title: Deep Country
description: The freewheeling indie-rock band crafts a sprawling, patient album that encourages you to lose track of time alongside them.

title: Traces
description: The San Francisco musician’s debut album sounds like a lost ambient-techno classic from the ’90s, but it’s far too vital to be confused with the merely retro.

title: Speak Daggers
description: The Iceage frontman’s second solo album carves out a niche in the gray space between folk, post-punk, and cloud rap.

title: Who Did the Body
description: The Houston artist shines as a storyteller over bouncy throwback Southern hip-hop. Though she has a beautiful voice, the ballads still don’t measure up.

title: Belong
description: On Melina Duterte’s first solo album in six years, the songwriter and producer reemerges with a poised set of pop-punk songs at bedroom-pop scale, with guest turns from Jim Adkins and Hayley Williams.

title: Amasia: Anamibia Sessions 2
description: The Brooklyn punk-funk lifer follows up the low-end abstractions of his 2022 album with an dynamic amalgam of avant-club music, post-vaporwave prog, and electrifying jazz fusion.

artist: They Are Gutting a Body of Water
title: Lotto
description: On its latest album, the Philadelphia shoegaze band strips its otherworldly sound to a raw, tender core.

title: Made by Dope
description: Backed by opulent production, the Detroit rapper turns in a comfortable, light-hearted performance.

title: Fatal Optimist
description: Mostly singing alone, accompanied only by her acoustic guitar, the Nashville singer-songwriter places heartache under a microscope on the third LP in a loose trilogy of breakup records.

title: Deadbeat
description: Kevin Parker takes a left turn onto the dancefloor and sounds quite lost. What could’ve been an interesting experiment is instead full of hollow songs and half-measures.

title: God Save the Gun
description: With longer, slower songs about addiction and recovery, the hardcore band embraces its pop ambitions with mixed results.

title: What I Want Doesn’t Want Me Back
description: On their second album, the Rochester-to-Chicago transplants come off like the indie-rock band next door, framing refreshingly candid songwriting in a classic, guitar-driven sound.

title: Vendrán Suaves Lluvias
description: Informed by multiple recent griefs, the Mexican singer-songwriter’s album grapples with heartbreak, mourning, and the desperate necessity of forward motion.

title: Some Like It Hot
description: Tired of their enigmatic rep, the London indie rockers embrace the spotlight on their most polished album yet. But the newfound pep in their step doesn’t always lead them to convincing songs.

title: Forever
description: With slyly artful pop instincts, the experimental London duo throws a raging 2010s-themed party.

title: Getz/Gilberto
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit a touchstone of jazz and bossa nova, the alchemical 1964 album that brought the dreamy sound of Brazil to an enormous new audience.

title: E•mo•tion (10th Anniversary Edition)
description: The pop star’s technicolor breakthrough sounds as radiant as ever on a deluxe edition, whose bonus material only highlights the magic of the album proper.

title: The BPM
description: Brittney Parks’ tense and virtuosic new album documents a life in motion, blending breakups and rebounds, dancefloor euphoria and everyday anxiety.

title: Nested in Tangles
description: After a 2024 breakthrough album about her father’s death, the audacious Vermont singer-songwriter squares up to her mother’s living absence—and, without her, finds her own way forward.

title: My Heart Is an Outlaw
description: The artist formerly known as White Hinterland celebrates self-reinvention, that most American of pursuits, on an album steeped in luxurious arrangements and the warmth of ’70s FM radio.

title: Goodness
description: The London singer embraces the darkness on her quiet and ominous full-length debut—it’s one of the most breathtakingly beautiful albums of the year.

title: Girls
description: The New York rapper’s new album takes aim at patriarchal violence and celebrates the power of love. Some tracks wane in focus and intensity, but enthralling production buoys the more cliché moments.

title: BLACK FRIDAYZ
description: The Chicago rapper’s new mixtape makes a bid for his own style, articulating a catchy, melodic sound with actual room for substance.

title: Fancy Some More?
description: The British singer-producer gathers her contemporaries and influences to remix tracks from this year’s Fancy That, transforming the album into a rowdy, star-studded celebration.

title: Pretty Idea
description: The R&B singer asks big questions about love and heartbreak on a ruminative album that’s retro in all the right ways.

title: Ace
description: The California musician’s third solo album is quieter and less accessible than her past work, but sacrifices none of her musical sophistication, adding newfound chamber-pop grandeur.

title: The Life You Save
description: On her third solo album, Jenn Wasner makes an offering of uncertainty, chasing newfound humility through deceptively gentle acoustic and folktronic arrangements.

title: Black Mahogani
description: Newly pressed on vinyl, the elusive producer’s 2004 masterpiece is a love letter to Black Detroit and one of the most ambitious house records of all time.

title: CORINIAN
description: The North Carolina rapper keeps things unpredictable on a playful, hard-hitting album.

title: psykotic
description: The head of rage rap’s new guard comes bearing muggy distortion, Auto-Tune chirrups, and synth-heavy adornments. Even as he refines his sound, the shadow of his predecessors looms large.

title: sleep with a cane
description: The London experimental musician is one of one. Her new, mostly ambient mixtape catalogs humor, absurdity, and grief with understated intention.

title: Worldwide
description: Studio production, wordier songwriting, and a vintage drum machine don’t slow down the egg-punk band. Their second album is rowdy and relentless as ever.

title: Life’s a Gas
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the electronic pioneer Wolfgang Voigt’s 1996 debut, a pivotal album that deconstructed rock and dance music into a singular, inspirational new sound.

artist: John Lennon / Yoko Ono / Yoko Ono Plastic Ono Band / Elephant’s Memory
title: Power to the People (The Ultimate Collection)
description: An expansive new box set showcases Lennon and Ono’s 1972 album and One to One benefit concerts. It’s a vivid document of a duo invigorated both by activism and the pleasures of old-time rock’n’roll.

title: SickElixir
description: Gnarled grooves and unintelligible vocals intersect at uncanny angles on the British producer’s new album, which amplifies his pugnacious style into a brutish, unhinged gestalt.

title: Don’t Trust Mirrors
description: On an illuminating companion to 2024’s Moves in the Field, the experimental pianist revisits its compositions in the glow of the dancefloor.

title: Diamond Grove
description: Recorded in an 18th-century farmhouse, the second album from the North Carolina collective is a vibrantly idiosyncratic deconstruction of folk music.

title: Tide Pools
description: Ambient synthesist Daryl Groetsch’s third album for Hausu Mountain is one of his proggiest and most challenging, a head-spinning trip through a low-res waterworld.

title: Vanities
description: On the debut full-length from her ambient alias, producer Barbara Braccini burns off the haze to showcase her gently swelling synths and hymnlike vocals.

title: Cosa Nuestra: Capítulo 0
description: Billed as a prequel to his last album, the Boricua superstar’s new release taps into bomba and salsa for an exploration of Puerto Rican identity.

title: Inland See
description: The Chicago psychedelic trio expands its cosmic, horizontally sprawling sound into a more songful direction—without losing the dazzling, hypnotic focus that makes its music so captivating.

title: Infinite
description: The duo’s ninth album—and its first since Prodigy’s death—contains reconstructed songs that impressively retain the two rappers’ chemistry, though mostly sound like a retread of the pair’s glory days.

title: Beware Beware Beware (More Lullabies)
description: The Detroit rapper and producer’s new instrumental collection evokes a fractious society of white-knuckled paranoia. Despite the bleak atmosphere, it’s a protest record at heart.

title: Taurus
description: A collection of outtakes from Joseph Stevens’ space-age pop project showcases his introspective, collage-like approach to composition.

title: A Written Testimony: Leaflets / Power at the Rate of My Dreams / Mars, the Inhabited Planet
description: For better and worse, all of the elements familiar to Jay Electronica listeners over the past two decades are alive and well in his new trilogy of mini-albums.

title: Kids Table EP
description: Conor Oberst and co.’s latest release feels shackled to nostalgia. Its songs rely on trite metaphors and obvious rhymes, but are briefly enlivened by collaborators, including Hurray for the Riff Raff.

title: Odu: Vibration II
description: Imagined as a journey into a cave, the Brooklyn-based composer’s new album is a longform fusion of ambient atmospheres, otherworldly soundscaping, and slow-motion horn solos.

title: The Life of a Showgirl
description: A dozen albums in, Taylor Swift’s never been bigger—and her music’s never been less compelling.

title: A Rhythm Protects One
description: Disguised by a fistful of new aliases, the London DJ-producer pays homage to the classic mix CD as a cornerstone of dance-music culture—and a showcase for the artist’s individual style to flourish.

title: Is This Desire?
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Polly Jean Harvey’s 1998 Southern gothic masterpiece, a bracing rock record of frustrated longing and austere beauty.

title: I Barely Know Her
description: On his full-length debut, the 20-year-old pop artist makes vague, melancholy music defined by big feelings and unsubtle influences.

title: UY SCUTI
description: The Atlanta rapper’s post-RICO comeback album feels engineered for virality and not much else. Even in wounded Southern pain rap mode, Thug offers irony and defensiveness without sincerity or style.

title: In Daytona Yellow
description: The UK dance producer sets aside the elaborate conceits of previous LPs and turns his attention to his guests’ voices—and his own. In place of house bangers, he offers a grab-bag of moods.

title: Goodbyehouse
description: Unlike so many of its neo-shoegaze peers, the Danish duo has no interest in sugarcoating its feelings—its sweetly melodic dream pop hides a wellspring of existential angst.

title: Through the Wall
description: The Toronto singer returns with a sleek, perfectly executed club record for the late-night crew. Her restrained vocals and velvet hooks are top class.

title: The Art of Loving
description: The rising British neo-soul star’s unfussy charisma and warmly assured voice carry her second album, a collection of classic-sounding, retro-minded pop.

title: no scope
description: Drawing from a playlist of 1990s radio faves, the alt-pop duo sink into a reverie of reverbed guitar, breakbeats, and weird funk jams that’s technically accomplished and a bit dry.

title: Vie
description: Doja Cat taps Jack Antonoff for a 1980s-styled pop record with standout rap verses. The playful synth-funk simultaneously suits her personality and boxes in her style.

title: Tender / Wading
description: Equipped with clarinet, piano, and a hard drive full of field recordings, the Colorado native goes back to nature on a bewitching album of melodic ambient soundscapes.

title: Kissom
description: The Lisbon native picks up the batida baton from her Príncipe label mates and runs with it, fashioning a boldly psychedelic, synth-forward take on the Afro-Portuguese sound.

title: Neon Grey Midnight Green
description: Neko Case’s eighth album meets the storms of memory and grief with a clarity of purpose and an awe for life. It’s a reflective moment from a songwriter in full command of her powers.

title: Michelangelo Dying
description: The Welsh musician composed her seventh album in the wake of fresh heartbreak. In songs that pair ornate arrangements and billowing melodies, she conjures mystery and surrenders to her own experience.

title: Nobody’s Girl
description: The songwriter and fiddle player’s latest record comes after her divorce from fellow Americana artist Jason Isbell. Comprising mostly ballads, the album is emotionally profound but musically narrow.

title: Here for It All
description: The diva’s 16th studio album is thoughtfully constructed and surprisingly candid about the present condition of her voice. It’s a no-makeup sound for a persona devoted to glamour.

title: More Is More
description: The London R&B singer’s new mixtape shuffles through retro sounds faster than a TRL lineup, marrying early 2000s bubblegum pop with UK garage and dance.

title: Joshua / Same Day Walking
description: On a dozen restlessly expressive instrumentals recorded between Marin and Reykjavík, the American guitarist finds turbulent beauty at the edges of the fingerstyle tradition.

title: Energy
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the lone LP from the legendary East Bay band, the original ska-punk album—electric, righteous, and unlike any other.

title: Twilight Override
description: The Wilco frontman’s sprawling new solo triple album is pure Tweedy: ambivalent and unknowable and funny and compelling. It is the thing he was always ramping up to.

title: Getting Killed
description: The recent metamorphosis of the New York band, led by singer-songwriter Cameron Winter, has produced one of the best, strangest, and most compelling rock records of the year.

title: Songs and Bodies
description: Mazelike and mesmerizingly slow, the Polish experimental composer’s new album nods to the sturdy rhythms and echoing space of 1990s post-rock.

title: w/ the Producers
description: The Dominican-born, Berlin-based artist embraces his status as the voice of dub techno, folding a stacked roster of producers from across the dance music spectrum into his subterranean vision.

title: Sysivalo
description: On a posthumous album from the pioneering Finnish electronic artist, Mika Vainio’s enduring interest in capturing the vastness of sound is distilled into pieces that feel both atmospheric and tactile.

title: SISTER
description: The exuberant EDM-pop of the sibling duo’s new album is dulled only by the sense that it’s all been done before.

title: History of Silence
description: The Icelandic group’s first album in 13 years dusts off a bygone strain of turn-of-the-millennium electro-folk. The acoustic textures can be appealing, but some twee habits die hard.

title: AM I THE DRAMA?
description: On her second album, Cardi summons the high-end sound of early-aughts rap and masters a style that is both wonderfully outrageous and easily digestible.

title: 8 Tips for Full Catastrophe Living
description: The prolific songwriter channels post-rock sprawl, electronic experimentalism, and percussive folk into meditations on domestic tension and strained relationships.

title: Orcutt Shelley Miller
description: Amid a monumental string of solo records, the guitarist forms a power trio that marches delightfully toward psychedelic oblivion.

title: Blurrr
description: The UK singer-songwriter’s sixth album is spectral and breathtaking. It’s a mood record of immense solitude, beauty, and free expression—with a crucial assist from the cellist Oliver Coates.

title: 41 Longfield Street Late ’80s
description: Four Tet teams up with the American avant-folk guitarist on a radiant, joyfully surprising album that folds together country, ambient, minimal techno, psychedelia, and more.

title: THAT’S SHOWBIZ BABY!
description: Finally liberated from the strictures of chart-topping girl group Little Mix, Jade Thirlwall cuts loose on a solo debut that revels in the glee of self-reinvention.

title: Real Warmth
description: On her latest album, made with a crew of Canadian collaborators, the folk singer-songwriter offers a salve against the horrors of the world alongside newly pointed declarations of outrage.

artist: Verses GT / Nosaj Thing / Jacques Greene
title: Verses GT
description: Longtime collaborators Jacques Greene and Nosaj Thing’s debut album under their new alias finds common ground in a balance of sleek club rhythms and introspective moods.

title: Body Lapse
description: Electronics and voice collide in this bracing collaboration between a computer musician known for hyper-detailed sounds and a vocalist who pushes her instrument far past the limits of language.

title: Catholic Boy
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the outstanding 1980 debut album from the famed Downtown New York poet, writer, and musician, a louche and witty hybrid of glam rock and ’80s gloss.

title: TRON: Ares (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
description: What’s great is that Trent Reznor sings on four new NIN songs. But besides that, he and Atticus Ross team up for a stripped-down and casually fun score that slots in nicely with the Tron composers who came before them.

title: Bleeds
description: Karly Hartzman leads her North Carolina band in another triumph. The careful songwriting and coiled performances wrestle with the many fiascos of life and love.

title: Girl Violence
description: Mikaela Straus’ third album is a sexy, testy chronicle of disillusionment that proves sapphic pop needn’t be just euphoric or pining.

title: Purity
description: Combining extraterrestrial R&B with head-busting percussion, the New York producers’ collaborative record establishes a frosty ambience that disperses as quickly as it sets in.

title: I’m Only F**king Myself
description: Written in the wake of her viral hit “Messy,” the British singer-songwriter’s third album centers her powerful voice and chatty, unvarnished style.

title: Pain to Power
description: Mesmerizing but somewhat disjointed, the Manchester group’s debut album boomerangs between hardcore, hip-hop, free jazz, and alt-rock balladry while rebuking oppressive power structures.

title: Play
description: The superstar’s eighth album is sweetly generic and half-heartedly ambitious. He’s got a couple of surefire hits, but he’s never sounded this lazy.

title: Mark William Lewis
description: The London singer-songwriter’s latest album is full of imagistic lyrics, foggy atmospheres, and moodily unconventional pop. It’s an appropriately cinematic choice for A24’s next step as a record label.

title: BRONTO
description: Canadian singer and songwriter Joel Gibb transforms his long-running indie-pop band into a Berlin-based subterranean house factory.

title: Songs for Other People’s Weddings
description: The Swedish musician’s companion album to a novel of the same name co-written with David Levithan is a sprawling romance bedazzled with vivid storytelling, absurdist humor, and ebullient flourishes.

title: Lick the Lens – Pt.1
description: For his debut project on Warp Records, the Swedish producer offers a mini-album of glitchy, pop-inflected IDM— the work of a meticulous tinkerer that still feels lively and social.

title: Let’s Meet at Junes
description: The rapper’s latest continues to open up his world with foggy scenes that capture a snapshot of being young, fly, and a little aimless in Los Angeles.

title: Breach
description: The duo’s eighth LP is a chaotic, maximalist pop-rock record that no one else could make, mostly because no one else would consider it.

title: Hell Is an Airport
description: On its sixth album, the Michigan band ponders boredom, burnout, and suburban sprawl in a set of densely hooky garage-rock songs.

title: XO Salt Llif3
description: A producer known for grainy, dissociative soundscapes takes a hard left into a hazy zone where ambient, emo, trip-hop, dembow, and more blur into an amorphous, unpredictable amalgam.

title: The Siket Disc
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit a surprisingly great instrumental studio album from Phish, an experimental batch of moody, improvised fragments unlike anything else in their catalog.

title: Who Is the Sky?
description: The artist’s new album of bright, bustling pop is positioned as a celebration of reasons to be cheerful. Often its fountain of optimism feels like a firehose of forced positivity.

title: Trying Not to Have a Thought
description: Philly’s emo-revival heroes are back to show us how it’s done. The band’s first new album in 14 years threads their finger-tapped riffs with familiar camaraderie and new social consciousness.

title: No One Was Driving the Car
description: On an album named after a deadly Tesla crash, the Michigan band channels its rage over greed, corruption, and empty promises into ambitious post-hardcore.

title: HAGEN
description: Grounded by the hum of cello, the new record from Mexico City duo Héctor Tosta and Mabe Fratti is a study in instrumental tension and mythic flights of fancy.

title: Friend
description: With her third album, New York singer and producer Jamie Krasner steps out of the fog and into the spotlight where dream pop, trip-hop, and shoegaze mingle.

title: Plunge
description: On harp, saxophone, and percussion, the London trio fuses composition and improvisation in a vaporous, polyrhythmic style somewhere between astral jazz and cosmic minimalism.

title: You Heartbreaker, You
description: Awash in menacing, libidinous energy, the Savages singer’s new solo album asks: What if the psychosexual angst of post-punk and industrial music were harnessed for pleasure?

title: SWAG II
description: Bieber drops off another 23 tracks’ worth of SWAG, his Dijon- and Mk.gee-assisted foray into alt-R&B. Bland and underwritten, the sequel magnifies the weaknesses of the original.

title: Essex Honey
description: Dev Hynes’ elegant new album, his first in six years, inhabits memories of an English childhood filled with joy, pain, and music.

title: Ego Death at a Bachelorette Party
description: On her third solo album and first independent release, the Paramore frontperson channels a range of experimental pop sounds to reflect on personal and professional grief.

title: Joy in Repetition
description: Drolly titled and curiously sequenced, the London electro-pop quintet’s best-of collection highlights the group’s deadpan humor, winning tenderness, and remarkable consistency.

title: Supreme Clientele 2
description: Once a peerlessly inventive rapper, Ghost has aged into ordinariness. His latest is a sturdy, occasionally invigorating outing, but the nostalgic framing only reminds us what he’s lost.

title: Clams Casino
description: The New York singer poses life’s big questions in the form of exuberant, classic pop-rock. His new album sounds like it could’ve been made any time in the past 45 years.

title: A Danger to Ourselves
description: The Colombian musician trades her typically fantastical subject matter for an album steeped in the immediacy of desire. The theme may be universal, but her sounds are as thrillingly out there as ever.

title: International
description: With its 13th and final album, the trio is determined to go out with a bang, once more mapping dance music’s energies onto tender feelings of longing, optimism, and nostalgia.

title: HEARTS SOLD SEPARATELY
description: Love and heartbreak are the Atlanta singer’s bread and butter. Her fourth LP levels up her sound, catering to her sensitivity and skillful pen while deftly accommodating her range.

title: East and West
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the curious, sideways 1984 debut from a New York City avant-pop songwriter who walked to her own beat.

title: Slipknot (25th Anniversary Edition)
description: Twenty-five years ago, a masked nu-metal band from Iowa crashed into the mainstream wearing jumpsuits and banging on oil drums. Their self-titled album is an uncomplicated, hate-fueled relic of its era.

title: Double Infinity
description: The cosmic folk band’s sixth album is their first as a trio. But they still sound loose, chaotic, and intuitive as ever.

title: Heliocene
description: Following a move from the Pacific Northwest to the Gulf Coast of Florida, the electronic producer pushes his low-key deep house in a warmer, more immersive direction.

title: The Prophet and the Madman
description: Working with producer Kamasi Washington, the Moroccan-born, Los Angeles-based singer channels vintage spiritual jazz on a solo record that feels fresh, literary, and ecstatic.

title: Burnover
description: The Vermont singer’s pretty great second album has got wit, romance, and sublime songwriting. It’s an unassuming collection of tunes that belongs in the heartland slacker rock canon.

title: Straight Line Was a Lie
description: On the Auckland indie rockers’ most incisive album, bulletproof hooks cloak gnarly emotional realities and cheerfulness always comes tinged with a creeping sadness.

title: Music for Nitrous Oxide (30 Year Anniversary Remastered)
description: Before Brian McBride and Adam Wiltzie became neo-classical post-rockers, they were collage-minded 4-track recordists. A new reissue of their 1995 debut revisits their spooky, abstract roots.

title: Man’s Best Friend
description: Delivering formally classic, facepalm-clever pop songs with a heavy wink, Sabrina Carpenter’s new album takes her persona to its apex, and maybe as far as it can go.

title: Hard Headed Woman
description: On her latest record, the Nashville songwriter mostly returns to classic country form. She plays to her strengths, mixes pathos with punchlines, and celebrates taking pleasure where you can find it.

title: Animal Hospital
description: The Chicago indie rockers’ latest record is a tangled nest of wiry post-punk interwoven with strands of noise and pitch-black cabaret.

title: Animal Poem
description: Through her graceful poetry and pristine instrumentation, the folk singer delivers indictments of modern indignities alongside moments of hope.

title: Ain’t in It for My Health
description: The young traditionalist channels a bygone era of country radio. He’s not trying to reinvent the wheel; quite the opposite.

title: Aurora
description: The New York band strikes a balance between its customary post-punk and brighter, more melodic sounds on an album whose lyrical preoccupations tip toward apocalyptic dread.

title: Fully Completely
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 1992 album from the preeminent Canadian rock band. It’s the sound of national icons coming into their own, and confronting the foundational myths of their country.

title: Tropical Dandy
description: More than just a love letter to exotica, the Japanese pop savant’s 1975 album is a celebration of the chasm between the real and the artificial—and the cliches that express hidden desires.

title: RA.1000
description: Terre Thaemlitz’s new Resident Advisor mix, echoing a performance in Brooklyn this month, interrogates Israeli genocide, American complicity, and dance music’s ability to seed change.

title: EURO-COUNTRY
description: Irish songwriter Ciara Mary-Alice Thompson’s new album overflows with comedy, tragedy, and self-lacerating wit. It’s a bold statement from a true original.

title: The Clearing
description: With producer Greg Kurstin, the UK rock band leans into punchier pop arrangements and a hint of 1970s nostalgia. Everywhere you look, their sharp edges are sanded down.

title: Live Laugh Love
description: Earl is on another level. The way he deploys his skill, humor, and encyclopedic knowledge of hip-hop has made him one of the most effortlessly deep and cool rappers alive.

title: Swallow the Knife
description: Songwriter Dana Foote’s new album channels messy experiences of depression and recovery into a tight, crunchy indie-rock package.

title: Walk Out on This World
description: On their first new album in 12 years, the California garage rockers mature in their own way with a set of jubilant, hard-nosed punk songs about disillusionment, lost love, and hedonistic pleasure.

title: The Passionate Ones
description: Marcus Brown’s remarkable new album beefs up his airy, omnivorous R&B, searching for a sound tough enough to sustain the daily grind and big enough to keep the dream alive.

title: Flux
description: Reuniting with co-producer Richard X, Alison Goldfrapp taps into airbrushed textures, shivery synth grooves, and sensual cosmic awakenings.

title: Billionaire
description: On her sixth album, the Canadian singer-songwriter is still finding enlightening new ways to use her voice. Behind the boards and on guitar, she’s got a formidable foil: Jason Isbell.

title: It’s a Beautiful Place
description: Nate Amos and Rachel Brown’s latest knotty LP is super chill and totally destabilizing. To call it their “guitar record” would be an injustice to the range and the humor they find in it.

title: Gush
description: On her most social, libidinal collection of songs to date, the Los Angeles musician combines cerebral synthesis with beats inflected by two-step, dancehall, and ballroom.

title: August
description: The New York guitar-bass-drums trio pairs the meticulous arrangements of ’90s post-rock—and the hazy vibes of bands like Khruangbin—with an ear for the sounds of Arab and Muslim cultures around the world.

title: Guitar
description: On his first non-instrumental album since 2019, the 35-year-old songwriter keeps it real simple. These endearing and affecting songs look at the wreckage of his past and imagine a sweeter future.

title: Songs in the Key of Yikes
description: After the lush, expansive contours of 2022’s Wild Loneliness, the Chapel Hill indie lifers sharpen their hooks on an energizing collection of punk-tinged power pop.

title: Dollar a Day
description: Behind its dollar-bin sleeve, the Texan songwriter’s new album plays like a workingman’s spaghetti Western drama.

title: Slanted and Enchanted
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit one of the manifestos of indie rock, a landmark 1992 album whose emotional peaks and diamond-sharp hooks are cloaked in fuzz, feedback, and elliptical lyricism.

title: Skintone Edition Volume 1
description: The late Japanese ambient maestro’s music is psychedelically heady and improvisationally homespun. A new box set collects his first seven albums for his own label, Skintone.

title: Blue Reminder
description: Conditioned by the awestruck pleasure of falling in love, and showcasing Meg Duffy’s effortlessly acrobatic guitar playing, their latest LP is their most confident, adventurous album yet.

artist: The World Is a Beautiful Place & I Am No Longer Afraid to Die
title: Dreams of Being Dust
description: The band that helped define the 2010s “emo revival” cements its move in a heavier, proggier direction, centering technical mastery and flashy production on an album that lacks emotional dynamism.

title: That Wasn’t a Dream
description: On their second record together, Mills and Palladino strip away all excess, building hushed, hypnotic grooves out of bass and fretless baritone guitar, and cushioning it all in copious empty space.

title: private music
description: The gravitational pull of Deftones gets stronger every year. Their 10th album shows them fully in control of their heavy, menacing, instantly recognizable sound.

title: A Matter of Time
description: The Icelandic singer not only invokes the traditions of the Great American Songbook; she indulges, interrogates, and goofs on them, adding a welcome spark to her retro mannerisms.

title: Who’s the Clown?
description: On her debut album, the Los Angeles singer-songwriter—who co-wrote with Gracie Abrams—pokes fun at emotional desperation. Her songs use specificity as a comedic weapon and, occasionally, a crutch.

title: Star Line
description: In the six years since his last album, the Chicago rapper has gone through the wringer. Star Line captures a new era of transformation and personal growth, but it too often feels self-conscious and shallow.

title: Love Is Like
description: The band continues its unchallenged legacy as the kings of normie rock. The swagger is unconvincing; the odes to reconciliation tepid; even LISA and Lil Wayne can’t rescue these songs from banality.

title: Khadim
description: Nine years after the group’s last LP, the Basic Channel co-founder’s latest collaboration with Senegalese players is an even more spacious, psychedelic fusion of dub techno and mbalax drumming.

title: AIN’T NO DAMN WAY!
description: Kaytranada slips back into dancefloor mode with a slick, relatively brief instrumental album. It’s the sound of an artist casually strolling into his imperial phase.

title: Music for Writers
description: The Brooklyn guitarist moves away from his customary folk and rock roots on an album of atmospheric ambient music intended as a companion to creativity and reflection.

title: Racing Mount Pleasant
description: Combining the panoramic sweep of post-rock with the intimacy of Midwest emo, the Ann Arbor septet’s debut is ambitious but underwhelming, filled with grand gestures that arrive like foregone conclusions.

title: Baby
description: The Los Angeles singer’s second album is a spectacular new vision of soul, pop, and R&B. His surrealist, collagist approach to songwriting stretches the bounds of sound and feeling.

title: Easier Said Than Done
description: The Tallahassee group crams hooks, angst, rumination, and studio wizardry into its debut album for Epitaph, with denser, darker songs that still make space for irreverence.

title: F.L.I.N.T. (Feeling Like I’m Not Through)
description: Filled with good storytelling, poetic irony, and a heaping pile of unforgettable bars, the Michigan rapper’s latest is his most complete body of work to date.

title: Songs in the Key of Z
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the sublime and bizarro compilation by Irwin Chusid from 2000, the first major attempt to define and survey outsider music.

title: Interior Live Oak
description: McCombs’ songwriting is in top form on his latest LP. Beneath the effortlessly classic-sounding rock and soul, his music offers a fascinating tangle of character studies, mythic layers, and barbed humor.

title: Hail to the Thief (Live Recordings 2003-2009)
description: Radiohead’s second official live album is a kinetic recreation of almost every song on their transitional sixth record. As a timepiece, its foreboding sense of unease is quite suited for the present.

title: Sunshine and Balance Beams
description: The Boston band’s ninth album restores its former post-hardcore roar while folding in strings and pockets of tenderness that suit the songs’ mournful mood.

title: Utero Dei
description: The new-age noise torchbearers deliver a 75-minute slab of molten tape grooves, spiraling drum circles, and eye-dilating samba trips.

title: lost americana
description: After a tumultuous year, Colson Baker sends his emotions screaming through the entire mainstream rock canon. It hardly works at all, but the album’s mere existence is genuinely fascinating.

title: GIANT OPENING MOUTH ON THE GROUND
description: Armed with nothing more than a gong run through a giant subwoofer, the Mount Eerie mastermind teams up with his former Old Time Relijun bandmate on an album of scabrous, mystical drone music.

title: SUMMERSONGS
description: On his latest album, the sexy-drill upstart refines his craft, trading bratty club antics for a calmer, more grown-up—but still decidedly libidinous—charm.

title: Vanisher, Horizon Scraper
description: The former YouTube rapper has transformed into an art-pop auteur whose ambitious vision is dragged down by some precious, overwrought songwriting.

title: Sound Bath
description: Originally released as part of a series of sauna-themed DJ sets, the San Francisco artist’s beautifully sculpted techno record doubles as a start-to-finish sex jam designed for bathhouse sessions.

title: Surrender Instead
description: Kevin Patrick Sullivan takes a meta-narrative turn on his latest album, pondering career success in candid, if somewhat straightforward, folk songs.

title: ABOMINATION REVEALED AT LAST
description: The prolific garage-rock icon and his bandmates channel their exhaustion with the state of the world into trippy psych-rock and furious punk.

title: Anyway
description: The New York chiptune group reinvents itself as indie rock lifers, alternating wistful looks back at its years in the DIY trenches with unsentimental critiques of modern life.

title: FLAVAZ
description: The Chicago rapper brings focus, patience, and compassion to a debut album dedicated to the necessity of maintaining hope.

title: Bugland
description: With Fire-Toolz’s Angel Marcloid, Jasamine White-Gluz pumps her shoegazing fifth album full of more textures, more ambiance, more chunky ’90s guitar. It crushes like a giant box of Gushers.

title: Pressing Onward
description: Combining bounce and Southern gospel, the New Orleans icon’s latest album offers a vibrant and unabashedly queer take on worship music.

title: Love & Ponystep
description: EDM producer and pony fan Zelda Trixie Lulamoon’s outrageous new album—her 21st—is a middle finger to copyright legislation and a love letter to growing up online.

title: Secrets
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the R&B diva’s 1996 album, a blend of grown-up pop and sultry quiet storm that reconciled Braxton’s soul roots with a sexier, more youthful edge.

title: The Making of Five Leaves Left
description: The songwriter’s 1969 debut was overstuffed with strings, congas, and piano. A new box set offers a trove of uncluttered renditions of its songs—and a more direct view of Drake’s early genius.

title: Black Star
description: The Ghanaian American singer’s latest album is a celebration of Black diasporic dance music—and a hedonistic, pleasure-soaked victory lap for a star at the peak of her powers.

title: when i paint my masterpiece
description: With an unforced approach and humble wit, musician and visual artist Alexandra Levy reflects on creativity, community, and writing a song even Bob Dylan can’t.

title: The Villain
description: On the singer-songwriter’s fifth album, they use post-breakup heartache to slyly confront stereotypes about masculinity and gender non-conformity.

title: Willoughby Tucker, I’ll Always Love You
description: The prequel chapter of Hayden Anhedönia’s Southern gothic epic gravitates toward sludgy slowcore and dusty, sepia-toned folk. It can feel like an endurance exercise, or a test of faith.

title: No Rain, No Flowers
description: After a year of professional frustrations, the duo—with help from a suite of collaborators—trades its gnarled blues-rock for blues-infused pop that’s almost unnervingly pleasant.

title: Love Language
description: Pushing back at the politics of hate and fear, the New York-based Pakistani American musician offers a radical fusion of musical styles, using the language of desire to envision a better world.

title: Metro Boomin Presents: A Futuristic Summa (Hosted by DJ Spinz)
description: The Atlanta trap architect shifts into the nostalgia lane with a talent-stacked double mixtape that’s like a crystallized memory of the club in the mid-2010s.

title: Radio Libertadora!
description: The Brazilian funk producer invokes the spirit of class struggle on his latest album of hard-charging bruxaria, but his MCs’ horndog chants are more retrograde than revolutionary.

title: once more EP
description: The New York rapper-producer refines his singularly unrefined style on a short, slaphappy new EP featuring a standout song with OsamaSon.

title: Mic City Sons (30th Anniversary)
description: Third Man’s new reissue commemorates the Portland band’s 1996 album as more than just a breakthrough moment for its young prodigy, Elliott Smith.

title: Electronic Dream 2
description: The original Electronic Dream recipe was a flash of brilliance so simple it’s impossible to reproduce. Fourteen years later, the sequel sounds like self-imitation.

title: PILLZCASSO
description: Mixing the pathos of Vietnamese balladry with the rubbery lilt of vinahouse, the Hanoi-born producer’s debut studio LP synthesizes an emotive new style of V-pop.

title: THE FUTURE IS HERE AND EVERYTHING NEEDS TO BE DESTROYED
description: The Detroit collective’s sixth album faces down the apocalypse with some of its heaviest music yet: visceral, vital, and filled with desperate, righteous anger.

title: Brute Fact/Home Truth
description: The Mumbai singer-producer’s new album couches hard emotional realities in echo-fogged guitars, bubbling synth-pop, bit-blasted percussion, and dreamy ambience.

title: Genesis
description: The Canadian rapper and singer takes an introspective turn, trading her raunchy bars and brash self-confidence for meditative—if slightly underbaked—examinations of uncertainty and identity.

title: Pony Express Record
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit one of the strangest, most exhilarating products of the post-Nevermind alternative rock boom, the 1994 record by D.C. hardcore alchemists Shudder to Think.

title: BITE ME
description: The TV and theater star’s powerhouse vocals and abundant personality don’t entirely make up for the uneven material and sometimes maudlin production of her second album.

title: If Not Winter
description: A shoegaze star born on TikTok scales up her sound with a full-length debut that’s beautiful on the surface but uninterested in challenging the genre’s priors.

title: Volver EP
description: The Peru-born, Berlin-based producer and singer’s latest EP—dedicated to the LGBTQ+ community—comprises a kaleidoscopic set of songs marked by rhythmic tension and a sense of play.

title: art Pop * pop Art
description: The California rapper and producer flips blog-era R&B sounds into breezy, eclectic tracks with the looseness of an experimental beat tape.

title: Alfredo 2
description: On the followup to the pair’s 2020 collaboration, Gibbs sounds unusually animated. The album is an effective demonstration of the rapper’s formalist technique—and prickly personality.

title: MASA
description: The Baton Rouge rapper’s first release since his legal pardon is a hyper-emotive data dump that churns through hunger, bitterness, boasts, and torment at breakneck speeds.

title: New Detroit
description: On his debut album, the Detroit rapper wrestles with his home scene’s growing influence on mainstream rap. He offers a portrait of his city that’s both loving and critical, grounded in stories that couldn’t have come from anywhere else.

title: Veronica Electronica
description: The long-rumored collection of Ray of Light remixes was a thrilling prospect. The reality is slight and ill-considered, neither an authoritative survey nor a dynamic reinvention.

title: Classic Love (ep)
description: On a new EP recorded with Nashville songwriter Luke Roberts, the guitarist picks up a bittersweet love song, revisits Constant Hitmaker, and covers Beach House.

title: Soli Deo Gloria
description: The Queens-born rapper is deep in his comfort zone on his latest project, sounding philosophical, charismatic, and imaginative as ever—if occasionally a little too cozy.

title: Edits
description: The Aymara musician’s hard-drive dump of DJ edits spins together Andean folk, bro country, pop, tecnocumbia, and more. Their hyper-charged mashups are searching, self-aware, and frequently thrilling.

title: Rockstar Junkie
description: In 26 songs, the Broward County artist draws a fully realized world where narcotized Florida pain rap feels both meditative and terrifying real.

title: I Love People
description: Pairing Laurel Canyon splendor with a surreal perspective, the Wand frontman’s latest solo album offers wry portraits of the strange characters and bleak situations that populate modern life.

title: Precipice
description: With a shift toward cleaned-up synth-pop, the singer-songwriter’s fourth studio album leaves her standout vocal performances feeling less distinct.

title: Juggling Dualities
description: The French producer’s latest album folds together new-age reveries, trip-hop head trips, and techno scorchers. It’s an adventurous demonstration of her range.

title: Autofiction
description: After nearly quitting his songwriting project, the Leeds-based musician returns with an album of gauzy indie rock. It recaptures his lush production style but sometimes feels overly cautious.

title: Dewdrops in the Garden
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 1994 swan song from the sample-happy New York dance-pop band that just wanted a great party and a better world.

title: Snipe Hunter
description: On his newest album, the idiosyncratic country star doles out advice, eats what he kills, and takes a trip to India. It’s his first record with no agenda in mind.

title: New Threats From the Soul
description: The rich and dazzling album from the singer-songwriter is filled with rambling, gambling characters looking for hope. It’s the late arrival of an essential new voice in American indie rock.

title: Cuntry
description: The New York songwriter’s rootsy, groovy new album is a proud and emphatically Black update on the American folk tradition of anticapitalist protest.

title: Love Is a Dog From Hell EP
description: In a world of chaos, the Pittsburgh quartet’s messy, mathy garage rock sounds just right.

title: DON’T TAP THE GLASS
description: Tyler’s ninth studio album is a brisk, single-minded, and snappy dancefloor romp. He skitters through electro, synth-funk, disco, and Miami bass not to reinvent himself, but to get lost.

title: The Emperor’s New Clothes
description: Helming the second entry in Mass Appeal’s Legend Has It series, the Wu-Tang vet leans into his elder-statesman status—which is precisely the problem.

title: Grady Baby
description: The Atlanta rapper brings a hypnagogic flow and a cocky personality to her DJ Drama-hosted release. But rather than an assertion of her star power, it feels like a mild-mannered love letter to home.

title: REST IN BASS
description: The Atlanta rapper’s second album is the platonic ideal of rage rap—diced-up lines and constant distortion, with enough vulnerability to balance the outrageous hedonism.

title: Adventure Club
description: Backed by a new band dubbed the Trauma Tropes, the Against Me! frontwoman pokes fun at minor indignities and major assholes in a set of buoyant punk songs.

title: You’ll Be Alright Kid
description: The fresh-faced 24-year-old songwriter behind one of the year’s biggest hits, “Ordinary,” rides in on a tide of post-Hozier Epic Sad Guy Music.

title: IIcons
description: The iconoclastic duo’s production is as jaw-dropping as ever, but its latest collection of techno-trance-pop club bangers veers curiously close to the conventional.

title: Hiraeth
description: After the gentle ambient of their debut, the two musicians carted zithers, guitars, and a reel-to-reel to the Polish countryside, infusing their avant-folk with a more bewitching sense of place.

title: Only Frozen Sky Anyway
description: On his 18th studio album, the eternally young-at-heart power-pop troubadour—joined by his old friend Jerry Harrison—turns his thoughts toward mortality, uncovering new emotional depths in his music.

title: JACKBOYS 2
description: The sequel to Travis Scott’s label showcase series is little more than proof of life for a beleaguered group of artists struggling to get traction, highlighting a label boss who’s doing very little to help.

title: Disiniblud
description: Alongside a suite of collaborators, the two composers (and longtime friends) present an ode to queer utopia rooted in electronic experimentation and ambient soundscapes.

title: Grace Joke
description: The Senegalese French singer and graphic novelist debuts on PAN with a moody, multilingual hybrid of R&B, alt rock, and Brazilian funk. It’s a spirited defense of the irreducibility of identity.

title: How Sad, How Lovely
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the nearly lost recordings of Connie Converse, a mid-century cult folk artist who wrote eclectic, ravishing, intimate songs years ahead of their time.

title: The First Family: Live at the Winchester Cathedral 1967
description: This early live recording captures the psych-soul trailblazer knocking out a night of contemporary soul covers. It’s virtuosic if not yet visionary, though the thrills are self-apparent.

title: black british music (2025)
description: On his XL debut, the British rapper-singer attempts to make the leap from bedroom tinkerer to pop auteur. Even as he navigates grief, Legxacy’s skill as a writer of concise, diaristic pop shines through.

title: WHO WATERS THE WILTING GIVING TREE ONCE THE LEAVES DRY UP AND FRUITS NO LONGER BEAR?
description: The Virginia rapper’s latest album boasts wrecking-ball momentum, fist-shaking incredulity, and the finesse required to fold in a more nuanced, intimate approach.

title: No Sign of Weakness
description: After a series of albums that played like coronations, the Nigerian superstar takes a defensive turn. The music still glitters on his eighth record, but the songs retread petty grudges and old beefs.

title: Headlights
description: Alex Giannascoli upgrades to hi-fi dad rock and sails home with a major label debut worthy of the all-time indie graduations.

title: traces of the ceiling
description: The Japanese musician’s first solo album in 26 years trades the exuberant electronic pop of her early work for hushed, diaristic miniatures for synth and voice that have the clarity of still lifes.

title: My World
description: The rapper-slash-influencer’s tape functions like a two-hander with her man. Despite boring beats and weak solo tracks, the two artists carve out an unusually romantic slice of drill.

title: SWAG
description: Pop’s youngest elder statesman continues to evolve his R&B sound by enlisting some big names from the underground. His seventh album is warm, blissful, and a little out of touch.

title: Suspension of Belief EP
description: The Netherlands-based drum’n’bass producer’s dazzlingly kinetic EP flips the script, channeling unpredictable rhythms into humid and mysterious new territory.

title: Do It for the Money EP
description: On his latest EP, the New York noisemaker serenades the No Wave movement he set out to subvert.

title: Neighborhood Gods Unlimited
description: On his sly, artful new album, the Los Angeles-based rapper confronts an inhumane information society with determination to claw back a sense of self.

title: Beside Myself
description: The Brooklyn-based DJ’s debut album is a grimly electrifying fusion of club beats, claustrophobic drones, and Middle Eastern percussion. The mood: weaponized pessimism with a sneakily playful streak.

title: Once Was Ours Forever
description: On his latest album, the Netherlands-based musician continues to refine his distinctive style of ambient guitar music, now bolstered by more confident playing.

title: moisturizer
description: The UK duo’s second album is a near-reinvention, an unbridled and clear-eyed testament to their songwriting chops that hones their vision and separates them from the pack.

title: All Our Knives Are Always Sharp
description: Assisted by Tricky, Space Afrika, and Ghostpoet, the Nigerian British musician turns classical influences and electronic production into an Afrofuturist statement of determined self-actualization.

title: GOODNIGHT HYPNOPOMP
description: The songwriter’s latest album, split between polished cabaret pop and slow-burning emo explorations, is a striking but uneven listen.

title: Boys for Pele
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Tori Amos’ divisive third album: a strange and unsettling amalgam of distorted harpsichord and bloody revenge fantasies born of ayahuasca, Mary Magdalene, and the blues.

title: Spun
description: With production help from Travis Barker, Nathan Williams’ latest album mostly sticks to the shaggy garage-rock formula he’s been doing for years and years.

title: Let God Sort Em Out
description: After 16 years, Pusha T and Malice return with a blockbuster comeback album produced entirely by Pharrell. It’s good, it’s different, it’s complicated.

title: O Que as Mulheres Querem
description: Even when the São Paulo-based producer laces his mandelão—a harsh, noisy subgenre of Brazilian funk—with hints of global club styles, his music remains bracingly extreme.

title: EM0THUG
description: The Tennessee-based internet rapper’s tracks pound, squelch, clang, squeak, and scratch. All at once.

title: Shakedown
description: In their other band, the Bar Italia guitarists make ragged, jangly rock with the intimacy of a post-rehearsal noodling sesh.

title: Different Rooms
description: Folding live recordings into improvised studio sessions, the Los Angeles synth-and-viola duo patiently unspools meditative soundscapes that are anything but haphazard.

title: Epicenter Imager
description: Filling atmospheric grooves with sonar blips and glitching percussion, the Dominican producer’s new album meditates on nature and speculative technology.

title: Tomorrow Comes Crashing
description: The Chicago band brings a bombastic energy to its third album, scaling up its hooks and digging deeper into dream-pop textures.
Kesha fills her first fully independent album with accordion disco, stadium-sized twang, and too many hooks to handle. It’s… confusing.

title: Interior of an Edifice Under the Sea
description: Slow, spaced-out guitar music is second nature to these two veterans of ambient and slowcore. Their second collaborative LP is warmly immersive, if rarely surprising.

title: Sins Aloud
description: The underground Atlanta rapper continues his ascent by synthesizing a couple decades of rap into his own off-kilter, off-beat style

title: Yowzers
description: The Chicago musician’s third album is a tighter, more intimate affair than its predecessor, framing soul-baring lyrics in disarmingly simple melodies inspired by blues, gospel, and folk.

title: Intermission EP
description: The Australian egg punks present a leaner version of their scuzzy post-punk on an EP filled with programmed drums and rhythmic riffs.

title: MARS IS ELECTRIC
description: It’s the Los Angeles rapper’s loosest, dreamiest dispatch yet, an enveloping and atmospheric collection that constantly comes together and breaks apart.

title: MVD LUV
description: In a set of sweetly ramshackle songs, the Uruguayan American singer-songwriter celebrates his home city and reflects on the challenges of stability after years spent wandering.
Nearly a decade after shuttering his A Made Up Sound project, Dutch producer Dave Huismans is back with a new alias, plunging even deeper into club music’s murky outskirts.

title: Tropicoqueta
description: The urbano star’s tender and expansive new album is a reverent tribute to generations of Latin music and the Latina entertainers who brought it to life.

title: EL CHITO
description: The Alabama rapper’s screechy, horny, ambiguously EQ’d take on Southern trap is both familiar and way out there—and only a little annoying.

title: Made in Paris
description: The influential beatmaker’s new album is exactly what you’ve come to expect, now with a French twist.

title: The Way of Time
description: Sampling a vintage radio play adapted from a 1926 novel about rural life, the Norwegian producer threads unsettling questions about climate change through his icy ambient techno.

title: BEAUTIFUL CHAOS EP
description: KATSEYE are the international girl group working from a K-pop blueprint. But what they’re making is just generic pop.

title: Violence Is the Answer EP
description: The prolific producer’s latest EP is both boundary-pushing and off-the-cuff, filled with unexpected genre mashups and uneven collaborations.

title: Sedonis
description: The prolific Japanese musician has been synonymous with harsh noise for decades. As he nears 70, he is as relentless, precise, and powerful as he has ever been.

title: Different Talking
description: The New York band’s sixth LP feels like a scaled-up team effort. The newly expansive sound suits Greta Kline’s hard-won self-knowledge.

title: Metallic Life Review
description: Mining its deep archive of sampled metal objects—gongs, cheese graters, nitrous containers—the experimental duo’s reflective new concept album pushes familiar techniques in new directions.

title: The Shadow of the Guest
description: The veteran New York trio continues its rich history of remixing and revising with a humdrum selection of choral renditions and ASMR versions of songs from their 2023 album Sit Down for Dinner.

title: Virgin
description: Lorde’s fourth album returns to the digital, physical sound of Melodrama. While rooted somewhat in her past, it’s a gritty, tender, and often transcendent ode to freedom and transformation.

title: A Tropical Entropy
description: The exceptional debut album from the Miami producer captures the lively, menacing, and sensual sounds of his home—a dembow pop record made for those muggy, electric nights.

title: Switcheroo
description: The eccentric Los Angeles songwriter reinvents herself with a kooky, conceptual, synth-filled dance record.

title: STARS
description: The Chicago musician mashes up metal, showtunes, drum’n’bass, prog-rock, and more, leveling up their overstimulating compositions with a more refined approach.

title: Tracks II: The Lost Albums
description: The sequel to 1998’s outtakes collection gathers a bounty of unreleased and largely unknown material. Offering unexpected, never-before-seen glimpses of the artist, it comes as a revelation.

title: do it afraid
description: On her latest album, the Brooklyn rapper, singer, and producer chronicles the labor of finding and holding onto joy in relaxed, loosely structured songs that evoke backyards and block parties.

title: Scratch It
description: On her most immediate and accessible album yet, Meg Remy trades the ’80s electro-funk of Bless This Mess for ’60s country tinged with Nashville and Vegas, embracing all her contradictions with gusto.

title: Fantología I
description: A compilation from Ecuadorean ambient label +ambién looks at hauntology—think Burial, nostalgia, melancholy, dead-end futurism—through a specifically Latin American lens.

title: American Heart
description: Benson Boone’s flair can’t make up for the fact that his songs aren’t very good and that he lacks a unique point of view.

title: Planting by the Signs
description: On her third album, the singer-songwriter depicts her Kentucky home with tactile clarity, populating her roots-rock songs with wry observations of small-town life.

title: The Universe Will Take Care of You
description: The British producer and Polish clarinetist take a playful approach on their collaborative album, their compositions buoyed by the power of mutual surprise.

title: VICTORY
description: All these years later, Rick’s sing-songy, slick-worded autofiction still sounds like he’s walking on air.

title: GULP
description: The Wisdom Teeth co-founder’s second album picks up the baton of the ongoing minimal revival, but his bite-sized house music is suffused in some surprisingly huge hooks.

title: Uncloseted
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we look back at a 2002 Detroit long player from a Black queer icon of dance music, an unabashedly gay and transcendent mix of house, ghettotech, R&B, and pure feeling.

title: Load (Remastered Deluxe Box Set)
description: Messy, overheated, self-indulgent, divisive, and literally seminal, Metallica’s 1996 album lacked only a colossal 301-song, five-LP, 15-CD, four-DVD box set reissue.

title: Raspberry Moon
description: On their first LP written as a full band, the New York shoegazers swing for the rafters. It’s their most polished and ambitious album yet, wielding a super-sized sound fit for super-sized feelings.

title: INFINITY CLUB II
description: Back for round two, the Toronto DJ’s thrilling bashment rave tracks temper turbo-charged riddims and booming bars with frosty electronica and mechanical garage.

title: Se Amaba Así
description: On their second album of smoldering synth-pop, Raquel Berrios and Luis Alfredo Del Valle examine a moment of friction in their own relationship with impressive candor.

title: I quit
description: On their fourth album, Haim break free from the shackles of whatever and cruise right down the middle of the road.

title: Desert Window
description: The English musician’s latest ambient pop experiments encase straightforward moments of ethereal beauty between vast expanses of understated tension.

title: Slugger
description: The Houston-born, New York-based singer-songwriter worships at the altars of Dijon, Alex G, and Frank Ocean—but sets himself apart by delivering rural nostalgia with startling sincerity.

title: Tether
description: On a striking debut LP, the Los Angeles musician’s intricate acoustic arrangements and intimate lyrics attest to the strength of her vision; the nuances of her singing speak to the singularity of her voice.

title: Phantom Island
description: The prolific Australian group lavishes its gently trippy compositions with orchestral arrangements. The results are often frustrating and overstuffed, but include occasional sparks of magic.

title: Lateral / Luminal
description: The duo’s debut collaborative albums use ambient and dream pop to channel hard-to-articulate feelings, but the concept feels more nuanced than their blissfully vague music.

title: Gadabout Season
description: Tuning into the meditative power of spiritual jazz, the harpist’s latest album aims to set her apart from her illustrious influences.

title: Aseurai
description: The New Zealand band’s debut album is a pop record that is alternately chill, cosmic, and cosmopolitan, led by the airy voice and grounded writing of Crystal Choi.

title: A Room With a Door That Closes
description: On her second album, the New York singer-songwriter searches for self-worth while impelling elements of folk, neo-soul, and alt-rock through thrilling hairpin turns.

title: Learning to Crawl
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we look back at Chrissie Hynde’s 1984 reinvention of her band, an album born of tragedy, chaos, and joy that becomes a no-holds-barred emotional rollercoaster.

title: Soft New Magic Dream
description: The Pittsburgh synth misfits reopen the haunted funhouse with their first album since 2018. The ooky-spooky hypnagogia hasn’t changed much, but it’s not stale yet.

title: Hymnal
description: Armed with strings, laptop, and a lyric-selecting slime mold, the Berlin-based composer catapults classical minimalism into the future. It’s a dizzying treatise on the nexus of living beings and technology.

title: Lotus
description: The UK rapper battled self-doubt and legal woes in the run-up to her sixth album; now, however, framed by uncluttered jazz- and rock-influenced production, she sounds in command and at ease.

title: Ripped and Torn
description: The young Chicago band crams its debut album with streamlined hooks and a reverence for pop, punk, and post-punk history.

title: Tha Carter VI
description: Seemingly written and recorded in a very expensive vacuum, the sixth chapter of Wayne’s legacy-making album series would be a disaster, if it mattered at all.

title: PRINCESS OF POWER
description: The Welsh pop singer’s sixth album returns to established themes of feminist empowerment and disco-pop maximalism. It often feels like treading water.

title: SALT
description: As its catalog comes to streaming, an overlooked band from the thriving 1980s Boston indie rock scene gets a proper reintroduction with Don Giovanni’s 10-song archival sampler.

title: I’ll Be Waving as You Drive Away
description: On his most majestic and sincere record yet, the Texas guitarist plays with grace and power, evoking the gentle emptiness of the American West.

title: Church of Kidane Mehret
description: The latest in the always interesting batch of reissues from the Ethiopian pianist focuses on her most explicitly religious songs, which are, incidentally, her most inert.

title: It’s Closeness, It’s Easy
description: From the bleary depths of shoegaze, ambient, and downer metal, Thom Wasluck’s first new album since 2017 returns with a pearl of hard-won optimism and persistence.

title: More
description: After 24 years, Jarvis Cocker and his baroque-pop band return to remind you, with rakish wit and horny wisdom, that your whole life is just one big coming-of-age saga.

title: Hunting Season
description: The emo band embraces alt-country on its third album, filled with stories that celebrate community, survival, and the weird and wild South.

title: Endling
description: In a prequel to his orchestral work about a post-human Earth, the Dawn of Midi drummer and synthesist imagines the last survivor’s final journey—and offers a flicker of hope.

title: Addison
description: The girlypop album of summer warrants comparison to Lana, Madonna, and most of all, Britney. Are we ready for Addison?

title: Squeeze Me
description: The Baltimore-born, Germany-based songwriter experiments with vulnerability on an album that mixes classic Hollywood stylings with evocative art pop.

title: Now That’s What I Call Crank! 25
description: Both nostalgic and forward-looking, the latest entry in the veteran DMV rap producer’s mixtape series offers an insider’s tour of a stacked regional scene.

title: Chuck Person’s Eccojams Vol. 1
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we look back at the woozy, ethereal Daniel Lopatin remixes that summoned vaporwave from the ghosts of the 1980s: a warped cassette tape on a timeless vibe.

title: Carrie & Lowell (10th Anniversary Edition)
description: Sufjan Stevens remains embarrassed by the raw grief of the 2015 album devoted to his late mother. For its 10th anniversary, Jayson Greene reflects on Carrie & Lowell’s place in his own life.

title: Never Enough
description: The biggest band in hardcore grows big enough to encompass electronic rhythms and flute meditation. Its new album winks to outsize expectations but answers to a higher calling.

title: Don’t Trust Me
description: The California rapper’s unrelentingly bleak tales of street justice have made him one of drill’s hottest young stars. His new mixtape is as striking as it is uncomfortable.

title: Trainspotting
description: The Griselda MC makes acrobatic rapping sound easy, and the Kansas City producer’s beats are spellbindingly psychedelic. If only Rome’s writing lived up to those displays of technical prowess.

title: Faith
description: The Brooklyn trio’s second album puts a contemporary spin on Y2K ambient music, trading the era’s cryptic leanings for warm, consonant tones and a spirit of emotional generosity.

title: Five Forever
description: The young Twitch streamer tries to become a rapper using the innate talent and creative vision of a Twitch streamer.

title: Let All That We Imagine Be the Light
description: The alt-rock veterans’ eighth album lacks the bite of their 2021 LP; despite typically expert production, the songwriting is noncommittal—though Shirley Manson remains a fierce, commanding presence.

title: Something Beautiful
description: With her smoldering alto, a roster of indie rock luminaries, and remarkable gusto, Miley Cyrus tucks into a concept album without a concept.

title: Evangelic Girl is a Gun
description: The shapeshifting pop producer and vocalist’s fourth album summons the chilly cool of trip-hop, but doesn’t do much to differentiate from the heavily referenced source material.

title: Get Sunk
description: The National frontman’s second solo album, made in the aftermath of a depressive episode, embraces a more positive outlook but sacrifices the specificity and dry humor that animates his best work.

title: Paradise Now
description: The Nigerian British pop star’s overstuffed new album shines when it’s danceable, complex, and ferocious.

title: Can’s Gone Warm EP
description: On her most fully realized collection to date, the British producer channels fleeting emotions into weightless, post-genre collages blanketed with tissue-thin layers of her voice.

title: Гільдеґарда (Hildegard)
description: Using modular synth and pre-modern vocal styles, the Ukrainian duo turns the music of 12th-century mystic Hildegard von Bingen into a chilling meditation on wartime trauma and the endurance of faith.

title: Black Hole Superette
description: The veteran underground MC offers another clinic in richly detailed writing and production. His latest explores the profoundly mundane, from aging to plum trees to snail invasions.

title: Alan Sparhawk With Trampled by Turtles
description: On his second album since Mimi Parker’s death, the former Low singer steps away from electronic abstraction and into the steadfast support of an empathetic bluegrass band.

title: Negotiations EP
description: On an EP of icy, chrome-plated pop that considers the body and mind as glitching machines, the Los Angeles musician seeks out a software update to cure burnout and self-sabotage.

title: Are You Experienced
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we look back at the explosive 1967 debut from the short-lived and revolutionary trio, one of the defining articles of rock music.

title: Fit for Consequences: Original Recordings, 1984-1987
description: A new anthology rescues the work of an obscure L.A. duo that—with an assist from Harold Budd—channeled the sounds of classical minimalism, new age, and new wave into brooding, hypnotic fantasias.

title: caroline 2
description: With a suite of mini-symphonies that boasts no shortage of surprising, mesmerizing epiphanies, the London musicians fully embrace their role as UK post-rock’s preeminent sentimentalists.

title: I Got Too Sad for My Friends
description: The mood is downcast on the English singer’s third album, but the record’s lush warmth and occasional touch of self-aware humor offer a welcome counterbalance.

title: I look at her and light goes all through me
description: On the Los Angeles producer-guitarist’s strongest album to date, he recasts his indie-rock roots into a delightfully dizzying collage of nu-gaze and SoundCloud rap.

title: Sounds Like...
description: On its third album, the country-rock group rips through a set of free-spirited barnstormers with such ease and joy that even its tales of raw feelings and perpetual malaise feel uplifting.

title: Caveman Wakes Up
description: On its fifth album of ramshackle Americana, the Philadelphia group finds revelation in the humdrum details of everyday life, turning weary non sequiturs into anthems for the downwardly mobile.

title: Quit to Play Chess
description: In a world that often refuses to see disabled people as all the things that disco represents—carefree, exuberant, sexy—the late California musician’s joyful final album is a necessary corrective.

title: Possession
description: Wrapping up a run of mercurial stylistic gambits, the So Cal garage rocker settles into back-to-basics psych and stadium rock on a record packed with feel-good anthems.

title: DAISY
description: The most reclusive member of the Spanish collective Rusia-IDK shines on a debut that’s as freakishly fun as it is sincere.

title: HONEYPAQQ Vol. 1
description: It’s not quite as wild as their debut, but the new tape from Detroit ghettotech’s breakout stars brings the low-stakes fun of a basement party where everyone knows each other.

title: Crooked Wing
description: Featuring Caroline Polachek and steeped in chamber-music gravitas, the Barnett brothers’ fifth studio album is spiky and dramatic, conjuring windswept majesty and esoteric lore.

title: Unmusique
description: The L.A. rapper-producer’s latest album abandons some of the fairy-sprite frailty of earlier releases in favor of an infectious juggernaut of blown-out sounds. It feels like the second coming of rage.

title: No Separation EP
description: The Mississippi band accentuates its flirtations with industrial music on an urgent, synth-punk call-to-arms that posits positivity and community as a bulwark against the world’s harms.

title: The Nashville Sessions
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we look back at what was to be the cult singer-songwriter’s seventh album, shelved and later released in 1993. Its deathly mystique captures the heart and soul of Townes Van Zandt.

title: Iz It a Crime?
description: The 21st album from America’s affable, couch-locked uncle balances occasionally tight songwriting with some utterly bizarre choices.

title: Big city life
description: The Norwegian duo’s slinky postmodern pop album approaches you at a party and whispers: Want to go somewhere even cooler?

title: Better Dreaming
description: After the introspection of recent records, Merrill Garbus and Nate Brenner’s sixth LP sounds refreshingly unburdened, with a newfound focus on jubilant vocals and danceable beats.

title: Land’s End Eternal
description: The saxophonist and synthesist’s latest solo album introduces a new character: an electric guitar that guides their amorphous ambient explorations toward ecstatic jazz.

title: Instant Holograms on Metal Film
description: The Groop’s first album in 15 years sounds like the Platonic ideal of a Stereolab album: cerebral, slippery, playful, and defiant.

title: LETHAL
description: Somewhere in here is the most hell-raising, heavyweight Rico Nasty album in years. But the tug-of-war approach to rap-rock doesn’t totally sell the vision.

title: Drained Strands
description: On its fourth album, the Berlin-based electronic duo continues to prod at unstable fusions of the organic and the technological, creating a rapturously dystopian take on dub-infused techno.

title: I’m the Problem
description: The country star’s fourth album stretches out over an absurd and needless two hours. But there’s an alluring thread of paranoia and fatalism hidden among the filler.

title: La Belleza
description: The Colombian Canadian musician brings orchestral music, traditional rhythms, and romantic separation into conversation to celebrate personal homecoming and ancestral communion.

title: Can’t Get Right
description: After his cameo on Kendrick Lamar’s “TV Off,” the Los Angeles rapper recruits producer JasonMartin for a G-funk revival soundtrack to his story of incarceration and aspiration.

title: pinkPrint EP / pinkPrint 2
description: Across a pair of EPs stuffed with samples, the Los Angeles–based polymath brings the halcyon swag era into the manic and noisy present.

title: D R E A M S I C L E
description: On her first post-divorce album, the country-pop singer-songwriter explores the new person she’s becoming. It’s a bright-eyed coming out aided by high-gloss production from Jack Antonoff.

title: I Live, I Die, I Live Again
description: On his latest tape, the Chicago emcee builds slow-burning tension with his deadpan delivery, a radically sparse opening stretch, and a B-side stacked with slasher-flick beats.

title: Yours, With Malice EP
description: On a relentless new EP of throat-bleeding industrial and EBM, the specter of violence that’s always haunted the electronic duo’s music comes fully alive.

title: Miracle Music
description: At its liveliest, the Portland post-rockers’ latest channels vintage Westerns and B-movie camp. But despite the addition of horns and sampled choir, it’s often a curiously understated affair.

title: Pinball II
description: The Brooklyn rapper and producer reunite for a high-energy sequel to last year’s Pinball. It’s a more digestible iteration of MIKE that still feels authentic.

title: Kate & Anna McGarrigle
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we look back at a trenchant and heartfelt 1975 classic by two French Canadian Irish sisters steeped in folk tradition.

title: Sketches for World of Echo / Open Vocal Phrases Where Songs Come In and Out
description: A pair of reissued live sets captures the singular artist’s playing and singing with uncommon purity. Less collections of discrete songs than extended fantasias, their best moments epitomize the essential spirit of his music.

title: Sincerely,
description: The singer-songwriter’s new album is a phantasmagoria of pleasure—the perfect complement to her talent for keeping her cool.

title: Performing Belief
description: On his first album for Planet Mu, the Big Thief drummer and laptop trickster turns his hand to globally informed dance rhythms. But the results are often frustratingly unstructured.

title: You Wanna Fade?
description: After a decade spent distilling power-pop heartbreak to its essence, the Portland quartet amps up its sound—and stirs up an even more turbulent emotional whirlwind.

title: Pink Elephant
description: Arcade Fire’s seventh album is a too-careful, too-canny exercise in restraint. It lacks the soul and spirit the band is known for.

title: the world is still here and so are we
description: The Welsh punks’ first new album in 20 years channels their abrasive sound and dirtbag attitude into a critique of the ugliness of modern life.

title: Top Hits, Ballads, etc...
