description: Under a gray sky of grief, the Detroit post-punks’ sixth album makes space for skulking grooves, shoegaze-y experimentation, and a Baja Blast that’s always half full.

title: Folkocracy
description: The enchanting singer enlists ANOHNI, David Byrne, Brandi Carlile, and more for an interesting collection of covers ranging from traditional folk songs, to Neil Young tunes, to children’s lullabies.

title: R U Saved?
description: The Detroit punk trio’s first proper full-length is a blast, but its abstract, evocative lyrics make it a welcome subversion of the punk formula.

title: But Here We Are
description: Dave Grohl gives himself over to arena-sized grief, reckoning, and resolve on the band’s most propulsive and purposeful music of the last two decades.

title: Lucky for You
description: Alicia Bognanno’s snarling alt-rock and sledgehammer choruses are blunted by the muddy production on her fourth album.

title: Roach
description: On her second album, the Los Angeles singer-songwriter trades her off-kilter pop arrangements for straightforward, unfussy compositions.

title: Early Grave
description: The Australian musician better known as Francis Inferno Orchestra trades his habitual house and disco for lo-fi indie that plays like a love letter to the eccentric records John Peel championed.

title: Horse Rotorvator
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the UK duo’s second album, a groundbreaking avant-garde pop collage from the early years of the AIDS epidemic that grapples with the nature of death.

title: Almost Healed
description: The drill rapper’s mainstream takeover continues with an engaging, guest-heavy, but otherwise run-of-the-mill album.

title: Bunny
description: Beach Fossils’ latest album distills the best of their daydreamy indie-pop with new wisdom and existential angst. But they’re just still as laid-back as you remember.

artist: Asma Maroof / Patrick Belaga / Tapiwa Svosve
title: The Sport of Love
description: The three improvisers conceived their new album while soundtracking a film for Louis Vuitton, but the results, far from being glamorous or overblown, are intimate and conversational.

title: Détwat
description: Twitchy, raunchy, and full of laugh-out-loud punchlines, the Detroit trio’s new album is the best ghettotech rager in recent memory.

title: Real B*tches Don’t Die!
description: Kari Faux returns to her Southern roots on a raucous, eclectic rap album that pays tribute to the ancestors, loved ones, and inspirations that showed her the way.

title: Walk Around the Moon
description: On the band's 10th album, Dave Matthews taps into his gentler side with the wisdom and grace afforded by age.

title: Freak Frequency
description: The Chicago post-punk quartet’s jittery second album rails against gentrification, algorithmic overload, and the bankruptcy of life under an extractive system.

title: Paradise Crick
description: Inspired by the great outdoors, the latest album from the Colorado musician and ambient artist is a gently psychedelic ode to all that is wild and wandering.

title: My Soft Machine
description: The singer-songwriter’s second album is headier and more dynamic than her Mercury Prize-winning debut, but its sharp writing is often blunted by its temperate sound.

title: Villagers
description: Tim Rutili has spent a quarter century cryptically subverting folk-rock convention. But in these songs—some of his warmest and most welcoming yet—he tells you just how he feels.

title: Sus Dog
description: Executive produced by Thom Yorke, Chris Clark’s latest album is warm and gratifying, offering the veteran electronic musician’s fragile falsetto as a graceful counterpoint to his intricate production.

title: Everyone’s Crushed
description: The Brooklyn duo's logic-defying new album threads anticapitalist critique, stoner humor, and a hazy undercurrent of fatalism into art-pop so mesmerizing it'll give you a contact high.

title: Romantic Piano
description: Built around wistful piano pieces that follow unexpected paths, the Chicago composer’s third album has far more personality and strangeness than its almost aggressively generic title suggests.

title: The Girl Is Crying in Her Latte
description: The Mael brothers are riding high. Their 26th album strikes the ideal Sparksian balance of madcap melody, labyrinthine arrangement, and stinging social satire.

title: Nothing Bigger Than the Program
description: With dusty, psychedelic production from Roc Marciano, Jay Worthy’s latest collaborative album is his grimiest to date.

title: Sheryl Crow
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Sheryl Crow’s barnstorming second album, a collection of restless pop-rock anthems with something to prove.

title: Happiness (Anniversary Edition)
description: This reissue of a 2001 album from Kieran Hebden’s post-rock trio captures the band’s shift from live instrumental jams to the more intricate, experimental style that he’d pursue as Four Tet.

title: Where the Flowers Don’t Die
description: On her debut, the breakout Houston rapper is determined to complicate her tough-talking persona. Not every stylistic swing connects, but it’s a blast to hear her growing into her talent.

title: Clear 2: Soft Life EP
description: The Atlanta singer’s subdued new EP is less interested in reliving drama than finding peace.

title: Wave Notation 3: Erik Satie 1984
description: Originally released in 1984 as a companion to Hiroshi Yoshimura’s Music for Nine Post Cards, this collection of Satie’s solo piano pieces is a cornerstone of Japanese ambient.

title: brain scratch
description: After finding an audience on TikTok, the Ohio producer extends their hypercute, ASMR-inspired sound into an album that floats between states of relaxation and overstimulation.

title: Seven Psalms
description: The veteran songwriter contemplates faith on a quiet, ambitious 33-minute suite. It becomes more surreal—and even funny—the deeper into it you get.

title: From the Cradle to the Game
description: On his sepia-toned second album, the Buffalo rapper looks back on a troubled upbringing while sometimes dipping into cliche.

title: Here 2 Stay
description: The 16-year-old Harlem drill rapper attained viral fame after the tragic killing of little brother Notti Osama. His debut mixtape is an excruciating contrast of teen celebrity and raw grief.

title: Tracey Denim
description: With a crisper sound and direct homages to underground music of generations past, the enigmatic London trio’s Matador debut is moody, moth-eaten record-collector rock that gets by on moody insouciance.

title: Kaytraminé
description: Kaytranada and Aminé team up for a set of sunny, funky party tracks best experienced with a Mai Tai in hand.

title: Could Have Done Anything
description: The Toronto songwriter returns with a brief and lovely alt-folk record, vivid and unmoored from place and time.

title: TALISMAN
description: The Pakistan-born, U.S.-based musician draws on the migrant’s deep well of loss and longing, weaving traditional South Asian musical forms into lushly textured folk, ambient, and dream pop.

title: Dismantled Into Juice EP
description: Beneath a shroud of dry ice and woodsmoke, the UK producer’s new record discards the conventional cadences of dance music.

title: Brandy Clark
description: Produced by Brandi Carlile, the Nashville songwriter's melancholy new album presents only a few facets of a complex artist.

title: End of Everything
description: As tense and exploratory as a sci-fi epic, the Los Angeles musician’s new album meanders through eerie, desolate prog rock and synth-pop.

title: The Answer Is Always Yes
description: The Australian singer-songwriter’s new album is a collection of hooky, blistering break-up anthems.

title: The Sex EP
description: Harrison Patrick Smith is the poster boy for a small New York club scene, but his sleazy, party-hard songwriting is not as transgressive as he would like you to believe.

title: The Big Mess
description: On their first new album since 2015, the onetime Brooklyn indie darlings turn definitively toward dad rock.

title: Heartbreak Rules
description: On a new mini-album, the Boston slowcore project pares back its sound to uncover new strengths and summon old ghosts.

title: Broken EP
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit a six-song EP from 1992, a record that alchemized the sound and provocative aggression of Nine Inch Nails.

title: Come on Feel (30th Anniversary Edition)
description: The uneven but fascinating sixth album by the Lemonheads gets a new reissue that explores the moment when Evan Dando was everything everyone said he was, all at once.

title: i’ve seen a way
description: The Manchester quartet’s debut album fuses dance rhythms, corroded guitars, and seething vocals into a transfixing blend of violence and transcendence.

title: Broken by Desire to Be Heavenly Sent
description: The chart-topping balladeer’s risk-averse second album is simultaneously overwrought and uninspired.

title: Resort Island
description: Since his 1998 breakout hit “Beau Mot Plage,” the German house producer has been associated with tropical idyll. On his first album in 12 years, he takes a more ambivalent look at paradise.

title: An Evening at Macri Park
description: The singer-songwriter’s second album is a raucous, messy, and celebratory song cycle about finding kinship in queer nightlife.

title: Gag Order
description: Swerving away from party-pop irreverence, Kesha collaborates with Rick Rubin on a spare and eccentric album about coming to terms with ambivalence.

title: Silver Haze
description: Jim Jarmusch and Carter Logan’s first album of non-film music is moody and deliberate, folding Marc Ribot’s guitar and John Ashbery’s poetry into thick slabs of psych-rock drone.

title: He Hymns
description: The UK club producer explores the links between spiritual devotion and bodily release, delivering moments of catharsis in chopped breaks and ghostly vocals.

title: Legacy Volume 2
description: The Chicago producer’s 2013 album Legacy affirmed his place in footwork’s vanguard. On a new collection of archival work, his loop-heavy tracks sound as raw, dizzying, and psychedelic as ever.

title: Monochrome
description: With confessional writing and immersive beats, the Seattle rapper-singer’s latest album is a more tender take on the player-with-a-cold-heart blueprint.

title: How Was Your Life?
description: The latest record from the UK electronic musician is built primarily on the guitar synthesizer, setting a tone that feels gently euphoric, whimsical, and bittersweet.

title: I Hope You Can Forgive Me
description: The Los Angeles-based singer-songwriter’s debut builds out her production while retaining the layered harmonies of her a capella work.

title: Romantiq
description: The glitch legend puts his past in context on lush, unabashedly beautiful pieces created with painstaking sample processing.

title: Orbweaving
description: On an intimate collaborative album, Madeline Johnston and Angel Diaz push beyond their common ground toward moments of grand catharsis and melancholy ambience.

title: Dog Dreams (개꿈)
description: With spine-tingling whispers and cavernous synths, the San Francisco-based sound artist traces the ghostly shores of her past.

title: Random Access Memories (10th Anniversary Edition)
description: Ten years have taken some shine off of Daft Punk’s gilded final album, but its unforgettable impact still echoes throughout the pop universe.

title: The Love Invention
description: Not quite a reinvention, the Goldfrapp singer’s solo debut sets her against sleek synth disco that she mostly complements rather than commands.

title: You Can Do It All
description: The Chicago band grapples with impermanence and loss on their memorable indie rock debut.

title: Try and Love
description: This 1973 album by a group of Lagos high-school students shines a spotlight on a Nigerian psych-rock scene that’s long been overshadowed by the legacy of Afrobeat.

title: Harsh 70s Reality
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the influential New Zealand band’s 1992 masterpiece, a rambling double-disc totem of noise rock that expertly balances tight songs and long improvisations.

title: Spirit They’re Gone, Spirit They’ve Vanished (Remastered 2023)
description: In 2000, Dave Portner and Noah Lennox recorded an album at home and self-released it in a tiny edition of CDs. But Animal Collective’s de facto debut is far more deliberate, ambitious, and sophisticated than you might remember.

title: Good Lies
description: The Welsh brothers earned a rep for festival anthems that bridge big-room functionalism with subtle experimentation. On their debut album, they go in search of transcendence.

title: Tête-à-tête
description: Combining archival material and contemporary reflections, the composer and sound artists’ joint album celebrates their long and resonant partnership in art and life.

title: Cruisin’
description: The Toronto quintet's colorful new album is all MIDI sheen and New Age cheese, the product of classy musicians working with the chintziest materials possible.

title: Daystar
description: The New York producer’s latest album bounces between rolling grooves and dissolving basslines. It’s primed for both the dancefloor and for getting lost in a headphone fog.

title: One Wayne G
description: This hours-long, 199-song compilation of mostly instrumental work is a canny product of our current streaming era. But at its best, it offers a glimpse into Mac DeMarco’s unique and evolving process.

title: ATUM
description: The Smashing Pumpkins’ new album is a trilogy-completing, podcast-augmented three-part intergalactic techno-libertarian rock drama!

title: Love Streak
description: The Atlanta rapper attempts to convey the subtleties of romance on his new R&B-inspired album. It sounds as though he’s never even been on a date.

title: Secret Life
description: Following his recent collaborations with Skrillex and Four Tet, hitmaker Fred Gibson teams up with the elder statesman of ambient. Unlike that anarchic trio, this project is dutifully, dully solemn.
Ed Sheeran has bragged that he wrote seven of his new album’s songs in a combined two and a half hours. It’s easy to believe him.

title: If Looks Could Kill
description: The Atlanta rapper has promised an unprecedented sound, but this overlong, monochromatic LP juggles a handful of shopworn topics and recycles gimmicks, flows, and ideas.

title: The Rat Road
description: On his first album in seven years, the UK producer embraces chaos: ten guests, 22 tracks, countless genres. Yet it can sometimes be hard to locate SBTRKT’s musical identity amid all the commotion.

title: An Inbuilt Fault
description: The second album from the soft-rock innovator is world-weary and contemplative—the music adopts a lush, earthy palette and his voice sounds better than ever.

title: Spalarkle
description: Featuring Caroline Polachek, Kero Kero Bonito, and more, the latest from the PC Music artist is giddy and psychedelic, with a mischievous sense of humor.

title: Naldjorlak
description: In two performances spanning nearly 15 years, the avant-garde French composer and the cellist Charles Curtis investigate the allegedly unmusical sound of the wolf tone.

title: Greg Mendez
description: The Philly singer-songwriter’s third proper album is written and sung with painstaking care and offers an entry point to his sprawling and satisfying discography.

title: Secret Measure
description: The Glasgow duo’s second record is polished and understated, seeking to offer reassurance in the face of stasis and uncertainty.

title: Bekka Ma’iingan
description: With an unpredictable, amorphous shoegaze sound, the Indigenous Canadian musician crafts their most opaque and open-hearted work.

title: The Truth
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the Philadelphia rapper’s 1999 debut, a dramatic and gritty album that brought a new kind of cred to Roc-A-Fella Records.

title: Anonym / Divin
description: Who were Tolerance? A pair of new reissues reignites the mystery of the short-lived Japanese experimental act whose shadowy beats and detuned haze arrived years ahead of their time.

title: Maps
description: The New York rapper reconnects with the Los Angeles producer for a masterful road-trip album. Humor and dread, weed and food, technique and style—billy woods is in full command of it all.
Featuring several collaborations with the Weeknd, the superproducer’s latest solo album explores the ways humanity may prevail over technology—too bad it’s drab and soulless.

title: Bird Hour
description: On their debut album, twin sisters Inez and Ella Johannson are immersed in their own charming, sometimes too insular alt-pop world.

title: Short Term Agreement
description: As the phonk sound that he helped develop has evolved, the Parisian producer has switched up his own style. His latest album feels like a grab bag of genre experiments that lack a distinct identity.

title: Erotic Probiotic 2
description: Filtering the sound of ’80s freestyle through a buoyant, time-warped haze, the debut album from singer/producer Marcus Brown is both captivating and elusive.

title: Lucha
description: The Mexican-American singer-songwriter harnesses the musical echoes of their ancestors into a gorgeous, dreamlike memory palace.

title: Museum
description: With patient songwriting and gentle arrangements, the Icelandic art-pop musician portrays seismic emotional transformations through resounding moments of stillness.

title: Slowly Forgetting, Barely Remembering
description: The Polish ambient musician channels deep-seated melodic instincts on her exploratory and enchantingly enigmatic new album.

title: All of This Will End
description: Fueled by earnest writing and exhilarating vocal performances, the Asheville songwriter’s third album aims for stadium-sized feelings.

title: Through and Through
description: On her second album, the Los Angeles singer uses her bluesy, soulful contralto to express a deep, almost ecstatic sense of loneliness.

title: Euphoric Recall
description: Raphaelle Standell-Preston’s operatic vocals and a string ensemble help the Canadian trio evoke the rush of new love, though some experiments go awry.

title: Jackman.
description: Without flashy bars or marquee features, Jack Harlow’s third album aims for clarity with soft, expensive beats and cloyingly intimate storytelling.

title: Gasms
description: Now 83, the soul singer returns with his first album of new material since 2009, and he remains as fixated on love and lust as ever.

title: Babylon IX EP
description: The London electro-pop artist takes a step forward after last year’s Bluff EP: The textures are richer, the emotions deeper, and her confidence more assured.

title: & the Charm
description: The techno DJ and leftfield beatmaker pivots to Balearic dream pop on her debut album. The tone is disarming and sweet, using nostalgia as a foil for spiritual fatigue.

title: dSX.fm EP
description: On a brief collaborative EP, the digipop artists pay tribute to ’90s electronic music while rediscovering the kinetic thrill of their past work.

title: Infinite Spring
description: Five years after indie-rock underdogs the Sidekicks dropped their fifth and final album, Steve Ciolek returns with a new project that recalibrates his ambitions while radiating emotional warmth.

title: catharsis
description: Led by guitar virtuoso Yvette Young, the California band looks beyond math rock with an album full of musical twists and emotional thrills.

title: Ryan Leslie
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Ryan Leslie’s breezy and lovestruck 2009 solo debut, a set of virtuoso R&B productions that emerged in a new era of online music culture.

title: Become EP
description: Five pleasantly familiar outtakes from 2022’s Once Twice Melody extend that album’s dream-pop sparkle and festival-headliner sheen.

title: That! Feels Good!
description: Jessie Ware’s sumptuous fifth album is classic disco revival done right.

title: Jump on It
description: On his first solo acoustic outing in a decade, the former Harry Pussy member shifts from deconstructing the guitar to reassembling it according to his own idiosyncratic design.

title: Everything Perfect EP
description: The 23-year-old singer-producer’s arena-sized pop-rock opens up a world of sensory pleasure on his second EP.

title: Heart Stopper
description: The L.I.E.S. label head makes a rare appearance on his own imprint, clearing away the lo-fi cobwebs and digging into tough, percussive dancefloor cuts.

title: First Two Pages of Frankenstein
description: With help from Taylor Swift, Phoebe Bridgers, and Sufjan Stevens, the National return with their gentlest album yet: a collection of airy, tender gestures.

title: Treasures: Solo, Trio and Orchestra Recordings from Denmark (1965-1969)
description: A new anthology of previously unissued performances covers three distinct facets of the jazz pianist’s career: his trio work, orchestral arrangements, and his endlessly inventive solo playing.

title: Son of Africa
description: A new reissue shines a light on the Nigerian session player, who brought his Afro-rock heat and slick funk to British experiments with West African music in the ’70s.

title: Devil Music
description: The latest record from the Austin trio is split in two halves: elaborate, hellish metal and dissonant chamber music.

title: HNPM
description: The rapper-producer’s new mixtape creates its own solar system, one where Hannah Montana samples and Jersey club orbit around the triplet suns of Afrobeats, emo, and rap.

title: OXygen
description: The 18-year-old viral rapper’s mediocre new album doubles as an endorsement for New York collective Surf Gang’s excellent production work.

title: Secret Stratosphere
description: Backed by a killer band of Nashville musicians, the guitarist electrifies and expands his inventive blend of Southern rock and space rock.

title: Future’s Shadow Part 1: The Clandestine Gate
description: The Seattle doom duo embarks on an audacious mission—a beautiful and melancholy three-album cycle about eternal returns and daily toil.

title: Safe to Run
description: Having traded New Orleans for Taos, the Michigan-born singer-songwriter offers a chronicle of her wanderings. The songs roll out as though she’d written them behind the wheel on a long drive.

title: ...So Unknown
description: The Philadelphia group’s metal-tinged style channels the physicality of a hardcore show with propulsive rhythms, call-and-response vocals, and floor-punching breakdowns.

title: Jōhatsu (蒸発)
description: The Ibiza-based producer’s first full-length in over four years, originally intended as the score for a Japanese documentary, nudges down the thermostat on the island escapism of his earlier work.
After the apocalyptic overtones of their 2021 breakthrough album, the Vietnamese experimental music collective finds hope in the fusion of rave music and eco-futurism.

title: Playing W/ Fire EP
description: The 19-year-old rapper’s boisterous new EP projects greater confidence, but its juvenile boasts can leave something to be desired.

title: Enys Men (Original Score)
description: Composed by the director himself, the score for Mark Jenkin’s experimental folk-horror film floats ambiguously between beauty and dread, creating tension through mystery.

title: Princess Forever
description: On their new record, the Chicago native fights the slow poison of the apocalypse with smooth R&B, galactic funk, and Afrofuturist fantasies.

title: The Notorious Byrd Brothers
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the Byrds’ 1968 album, the best and most cohesive project from a classic rock band in constant flux with the changing times.

title: Since Time Is Gravity
description: Bringing together players from across Chicago’s improv community, Joshua Abrams’ ensemble folds elements of jazz and North African music into mesmerizing pieces that hint at eternity.

title: Fuse
description: After 24 years, the electronic pop duo returns with a moving, handsome album that tells a sophisticated story about recapturing innocence.

title: Yallah Beibe
description: The multilingual East African rapper embraces a crisp, confident sound on her second full-length.

title: Big Picture
description: The third album from the Bristol singer-songwriter furnishes complex storytelling in cozy, lived-in atmospheres.

title: Wickman Stickman
description: Though it’s less outlandish than previous projects, the Queens rapper’s new album confirms his status as one of New York drill’s most important innovators.

title: Enigmatic Society
description: The hybrid jazz supergroup featuring Kamasi Washington, Robert Glasper, Terrace Martin, and more keeps it exquisitely sparse and supremely chill.

title: Härvest
description: The Philadelphia punk band couches its revolutionary anthems in winking medieval imagery, flirting with camp as they sharpen the guillotine’s blade.

title: Have Mercy on Us
description: The Chicago-born rapper-producer’s new mixtape is woozy but tight, flaunting its open infatuation with all kinds of rap.

title: Pila’e Teteo
description: The Dominican artist’s terrific second album runs at a breakneck pace and excels at two of the elements that make dembow so irresistible: hooks and humor.

title: Henry St.
description: On his first album with a proper band, the Swedish singer-songwriter sounds great, even as he says so very little.

title: The Window Is the Dream
description: On her second album, the Texas-born, Charlottesville-based singer-songwriter traces generous circles around nebulous feelings; her songs seem to emerge from deep stillness.

title: The Night Safari EP
description: More than a decade after his last album, the UK singer-songwriter grapples with an intense period of personal upheaval in songs that return to the melancholy, idiosyncratic sound of his early work.

title: Covers Vol. 1
description: The singer-songwriter pays tribute to Elliott Smith, Nick Drake, Arthur Russell, and more on a set of covers that play like quiet seances.

title: Holy Red Wagon
description: The second album from the Albany freak-folk group is vivid and dreamlike, revealing a meticulous attention to detail.

title: Brothers in Christ EP
description: Kindred spirits in the I-35 noise-rock scene share a split EP rooted in the ’90s underground; the normally pummeling Chat Pile indulge some surprisingly tuneful indie influences.

title: Why Does the Earth Give Us People to Love?
description: On her brutally honest debut album, the Chicago singer-songwriter takes folk music and bends it to her will, exploring agony and adoration in equal measure.

title: SPEED RUN
description: The New York hyperpop duo’s True Panther debut is crammed full of ideas but feels creatively vacant: the soundtrack to a party where everyone’s pretending to have fun.

title: Call Me Terry
description: The Australian post-punk band takes aim at the crooks and scammers on its most political album yet.

title: The Smell of Our Own (20th Anniversary Edition)
description: Twenty years ago, Joel Gibb joyfully preached a vision of gay revolution. His group’s debut offered a prescient vision of the currents that power queer culture today.

title: International Pop Overthrow
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the power-pop trio’s 1991 debut, a scrappy, diamond-sharp, hook-filled attempt to become the biggest rock band out of Chicago.

title: Forever Means EP
description: A new EP of four songs recorded during sessions for last year’s Big Time forms a bridge between the singer-songwriter’s past and present.

title: Multitudes
description: Feist’s quietest album to date is warm and comforting throughout, but really peaks when it gets fuller, weirder, and more unpredictable.

title: Brand New Life
description: Pioneering harpist Dorothy Ashby established the instrument’s place in post-bop jazz. Younger pays tribute to Ashby’s achievements, covering her songs and tracing her influence on contemporary hip-hop.

title: Frame & Canvas (25th Anniversary Edition)
description: On a remastered and remixed edition, the brilliant third record by the Champaign, Illinois band represents the platonic ideal for what Midwest emo has to offer.

title: Blondshell
description: Sabrina Teitelbaum’s self-titled debut is a candid snapshot of early adulthood, a cruel rotation of bad substances, scummy men, and friendship anxieties.

title: 72 Seasons
description: At 77 minutes, Metallica’s eleventh studio album delivers everything you could want from a Metallica album in 2023 and so much more. Too much more.

title: Never Enough
description: The Canadian R&B singer’s sleepy, erratically experimental third album proves that good old-fashioned love songs and heartbreak ballads are still his strong suit.

title: Let Me Update My Status
description: Like a corrupted file ripped straight from LimeWire, the Houston rapper’s new tape smashes together crunk, snap, and SouljaBoy ad-libs into a blast of nostalgia that’s never stuck in the past.

title: On the Romance of Being
description: After training as a traditional Nguni spiritual healer, the South African musician returns with a 13-piece band for an album of divine orchestral soul.

title: Sremm 4 Life
description: The rap radio pleasure-seekers grow up, exploring new sounds and real-world themes. It’s sometimes formulaic, but maturity looks good on them.

title: Crystal Vision
description: The English electronic artist pays tribute to his inspirations while maintaining his distinct, masterful sound.

title: muted colors
description: The Colorado percussionist’s debut solo album is a glitchy sound collage where drums resemble saxophones and voice memos share space with guest vocalists.

title: Mythologies
description: In his first solo project since the group’s dissolution, the former Daft Punk member swaps his customary synths for a full orchestra—but some old habits die hard.

title: No Highs
description: The veteran ambient musician pushes back at the hollowing out of the form with a burly, physically imposing release peppered with moments of gentle beauty.

title: The Complete Scepter Singles 1962-1973
description: This compilation is an ideal introduction to a defining voice of the ’60s: a sweeping survey of pop songs as prayers for compassion, consolation, and commitment

title: When It’s Going Wrong
description: The short but well-developed debut from the Polish singer features close collaborations with the trip-hop luminary as they conjure a hushed, alluring atmosphere.

title: With a Hammer
description: Yaeji’s debut channels a lifetime’s worth of anger into an airy blend of synth-pop, jazz, techno, and ambient. It’s a generous, understated exploration of rage as a source of creative renewal.

title: Gallows Wine
description: Following the blues influences of his last solo album, the K Records founder’s new record offers a restless pastiche of primitive rock’n’roll, rockabilly, cowpoke ditties, and living-room dub.

title: Stereo Mind Game
description: The moody London indie folk trio return with a stripped-back record inspired by long-distance longing.

title: Instant Vintage
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Raphael Saadiq’s 2002 debut, a meticulously crafted record that bridged generations of soul and R&B.

title: The Upper Cuts (2023 Edition)
description: Alan Braxe’s iconic monograph of French house, originally released in 2005, channels livewire synths, sculpted drums, and tension-stoking filters into a steady succession of dopamine hits.

title: Rat Saw God
description: Wednesday’s noisy, rangy sound finds a home in the quiet, lonely corners of America. Their outstanding new album is why they’re one of the best indie rock bands around.

title: Reclaim
description: The Spanish producer’s evocative debut album exists in an interzone where the natural world seems forever on the cusp of swallowing up the constructed one.

title: Bastard Jargon
description: Where the South African singer-songwriter’s work was tinged with melancholy, their new album, executive produced by Nile Rodgers, renders carnal ecstasy in bright tones and major keys.

title: Leather Blvd.
description: The producer and rapper pay homage to urbane Black cool with leisurely collages of neo-soul, jazz, and rap. It’s a nice vibe, but the vision wears thin.

title: Imagine This Is a High Dimensional Space of All Possibilities
description: After experiments in free jazz and psychedelia, the UK producer reckons with the rave music of his youth. It’s a utopian project that melds dance music’s forms with an organic sensibility.

title: Sundown
description: Teaming with producer John Carroll Kirby, the R&B singer sets an idyllic, spiritual mood while contemplating the weight of the world.

title: Duo Deleite
description: Two of Puerto Rico’s most promising independent rappers join forces for a summer-ready album, threading samba and ballroom into the worlds of R&B and reggaeton.

title: Call Me If You Get Lost: The Estate Sale
description: The deluxe edition is a continuation of the album’s block-spinning flexes, the pertinent one being that even his B-sides are unforgettable.

title: Continue as a Guest
description: On a sleek and subdued new album, A.C. Newman takes the lead and reflects on the isolation of modern life.

title: Let the Moon Be a Planet
description: The guitarist and the pianist collaborate for an album of gentle, edgeless improvisations.

title: Jasmine on a Night in July
description: Falling somewhere between Bill Frisell’s basement and the Mediterranean Sea, the debut from this instrumental Brooklyn trio marks a promising arrival.

title: My Vision
description: The teenage Tallahassee rapper fast-tracks a summer-ready debut mixtape that’s in touch with his Florida roots.

title: Peach Blossom
description: The Polish composer’s sumptuous new album draws on Renaissance-era vocal music, contemporary theater, and the uncanny magic of Auto-Tune.

title: Gisela
description: The Brooklyn-based, Barcelona-born musician’s debut album is a dense but cohesive statement on duality, equally shaped by Catalan identity and future-leaning cosmic pop.

title: Miracle-Level
description: Recorded in single takes with minimal overdubs, the San Francisco band’s latest album—its first sung entirely in Satomi Matsuzaki’s native Japanese—is a confident set of small epiphanies.

title: The Great Escape
description: On their first joint album, the veteran producer’s relaxed tempos and the San Francisco rapper’s coolheaded flows slide together with easy fluidity.

title: Honky Château (50th Anniversary Edition)
description: A new reissue of Elton John’s pivotal seventh album highlights its whimsical, rough-hewn charm just as the artist was becoming a superstar.

title: 绿帽 Green Hat
description: On his second album, the Malaysian-born, Shanghai- and Taipei-based producer interweaves industrial-strength techno and Asian instruments into a potent expression of rage and anxiety.

title: Warren Zevon
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Warren Zevon’s 1976 breakthrough, an unforgettable collection of rock songs as short stories set in a seedy, mythological American West.

title: The Price of Progress
description: The Brooklyn band’s ninth album is vivid and weird: a celebration of second winds, unlikely comebacks, and undying rock’n’roll dreams.

title: The Record
description: Julien Baker, Phoebe Bridgers, and Lucy Dacus devote their debut record to their singular bond. Each amplifies the other’s songwriting, enriches the detail, and heightens the emotion.

title: In Pieces
description: Beyoncé protégé Chloe Bailey is a generational talent, but the generic songwriting and chemistry-free features on her solo debut don’t make the case.

title: Only Constant
description: The New Jersey band’s debut LP sticks to time-tested hardcore formulas, but even within those bounds—and in under 17 minutes—the group discovers whole universes.

title: Rookie’s Bustle
description: Armed with breakbeats, gnarled riffs, and her most uplifting songwriting yet, the Black Dresses musician maps an arduous path toward love and security.

title: Generational Curse
description: The battled-tested L.A. rapper’s debut combines technical skill and narrative ambition for a gripping album about broken systems and the drudgery of art always imitating life.

title: Exodus the North Star EP
description: The Brooklyn singer and songwriter sounds more hopeful and more vulnerable on a mellow, reggae-infused companion EP to last year’s album.

title: Punter
description: The Australian punk band refuses to forgive and forget on a nuanced, ambitious punk record.

title: Drag on Girard
description: On its first album in seven years, the Philly band jams and shreds and searches for a groove.

title: Since I Have a Lover
description: The East Atlanta artist is typically an excellent mood curator, but on his first full-length in five years, he feels uncharacteristically dull.
Picking up the baton from acolytes like !!! and LCD Soundsystem, Brit-funk originals ACR enter their fifth decade with an energized take on an old sound.

title: 3D & the Holograms
description: The Australian band sets tales of the dystopian future to punk rock that’s nasty, cartoonish, and short.

artist: Arooj Aftab / Vijay Iyer / Shahzad Ismaily
title: Love in Exile
description: Recording live in the studio with just voice, keys, and bass, the trio achieves an almost telepathic connection: three seasoned musicians breathing together as a single organism.

title: Ways of Knowing
description: On Sage Elsesser’s Def Jam debut, smooth gospel samples set the tone for a worshipful exploration of the ancestral wisdom that guides his present.

title: The Art of Forgetting
description: Stylistic shifts and personal reinvention have become par for the course for this New York singer-songwriter. But on their new album, they turn uncharacteristically self-reflective.

title: Scaring the Hoes
description: The iconoclastic rappers collide on a JPEG-produced joint album that plays things fast and loose.

title: Requiem for Jazz
description: The Chicago composer and clarinetist’s latest album interrogates the supposed “death” of jazz. Structured as an Afrofuturist requiem, it offers an impassioned look at jazz’s role in Black history.
On a wildly ambitious 80-minute opus, Haela Ravenna Hunt-Hendrix’s shapeshifting metal band reaches its most radiant incarnation yet.

title: Amor Prohibido
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the Tejano star’s landmark 1994 album, her magnum opus that redefined the sound of Latin pop.

title: Live at Bush Hall
description: Over a three-night stand in London last December, the UK group evolved from rousing post-punks to an irreverent dinner-theater act. Yet the soundtrack of all-new songs feels like a natural evolution.

title: Did You Know That There’s a Tunnel Under Ocean Blvd
description: The singer-songwriter’s ninth album arrives as a sweeping, sterling, often confounding work of self-mythology and psychoamericana: Lana’s in the zone.

title: False Lankum
description: The Dublin group has spent a decade making folk music sound foreign and transfixing. Its spellbinding new album uncovers eerie new depths in centuries-old forms.

title: The Town That Cursed Your Name
description: The latest record from Glenn Donaldson chronicles the ups-and-downs of music industry lifers, searching for pockets of transcendence amid ennui.

title: Memento Mori
description: On their most engaged album in a quarter-century, Martin Gore and Dave Gahan find that familiar sounds can offer several new ways forward.

title: Due in Color
description: On his latest album, the prolific Turin producer aims to hybridize dancefloor potency and dreamy ambience.

title: YIAN
description: On her debut album, the London-based cellist and composer explores her experiences as a child of the Chinese diaspora. Musically and conceptually, the record evokes hazy, in-between spaces.

title: MAD
description: The Louisville rapper has a keen talent for bridging regional styles. The uninspired beats on his new album fail to light up the map.

title: With Love From
description: The sister duo takes influence from Fleetwood Mac on a breezy album defined by warm harmonies and easygoing pop melodies.

title: Till I’m Dead
description: On his supposed debut album, the hyper-prolific Rochester rapper upgrades his fidelity and sharpens his focus.

title: Songs of Surrender
description: Spearheaded by the Edge, this collection of stripped-down, re-imagined U2 songs is a frustrating missed opportunity.

title: Bad Premonition EP
description: The Colombian-Canadian singer-songwriter’s latest EP refines her stylish, reflective pop but leans on too uniform of a palette.

title: Voyageur
description: A collection of songs the iconic Malian guitarist and his collaborators recorded at jam sessions and concert rehearsals between 1991 and 2004 reflects the timeless vitality of his music.

title: Joe Ely / Honky Tonk Masquerade / Down on the Drag
description: New remasters of the country singer’s first three solo albums highlight his unique blend of honky-tonk, rockabilly, and Tex-Mex influences—a sound that could only have come from his native West Texas.

title: Fantasy
description: On his ninth album, Anthony Gonzalez is still trying to recapture childhood’s pangs of wonderment. This time, his nostalgia leads him back to the youthful drama of his own Before the Dawn Heals Us.

title: Say What You Like
description: On his first new album since 2018, the Canadian songwriter with the gentle country lilt laments almost everything.

title: Eye of Delirious
description: Ganna Bryzhata’s ethereal, shape-shifting electroacoustic experiments feel equally conducive to beatific calm and deep melancholy.

title: Kosogor
description: On their first official duo project, longtime collaborators Kedr Livanskiy and Flaty trade their customary dance influences for atmospheric dream pop steeped in folk, goth, and trip-hop.

title: …And Don’t the Kids Just Love It
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit a genre-defining debut from 1981 featuring the acerbic Dan Treacy and his clever, fragile, timeless songs.

title: Less
description: The London slowcore band’s second album is a gentle refinement with an atmosphere of loss.

title: Praise a Lord Who Chews but Which Does Not Consume; (Or Simply, Hot Between Worlds)
description: The art-rock auteur’s latest album is a glistening, richly detailed world that feels like a culmination of their ever-escalating talent and ambition.

title: V
description: On his fifth album, Ruban Nielson accompanies some of his strongest songwriting and performances to date with foggy production that makes the whole thing feel like a long, rummy sigh.

title: 1822.demos
description: The Irish-Filipino singer’s elegant new mixtape blends soulful grooves with sci-fi dreaminess.

title: The Complete Singles
description: This collection tells the full story of a Madchester band that’s never quite gotten its due, documenting tentative forays into acid house alongside tight, ’60s-inspired songwriting.

title: 10,000 gecs
description: The madcap duo’s second album is about many things—junk food, being dumb, the ska revival—but mostly it’s about two savants making pop music sound absurdly fun.

title: A New Tomorrow
description: Injecting blastbeats and mosh-worthy riffs with classic soul and reggae samples, the Los Angeles hardcore band’s debut insists on a complex and irreducible vision of Blackness.

title: Outerwear SZN 3
description: Loaded with snarled rhymes and hyperlocal references, the Brooklyn rapper’s latest tape is a thrilling, larger-than-life depiction of New York hip-hop cornerstones.

title: Oh Me Oh My
description: At 73, the outsider artist has made his most ambitious and approachable album: an extraordinary aural memoir that tells a cosmic story of survival.

title: Glim
description: This digital-exclusive album from the Berlin-based Kenyan artist sounds blank and unrevealing but opens up to reveal a wealth of detail. It’s prickly, insidious, and at times grueling.

title: Post-American
description: On its debut album, the Mississippi synth-punk band hones a sound characterized by unlikely combinations: frenzied rhythms and tranquil synths, blistering riffs and hopeful lyrics.

title: Radial Gate
description: North Carolina singer-songwriter Justin Morris writes with a sense of offhand intimacy, shading familiar Appalachian guitar textures with memory and ambiguity.

title: Endless Summer Vacation
description: Behind its carefree title, Miley Cyrus’ eighth album is an edgeless and synthetic collection of disco-pop bummer jams.

title: Blacklips Bar: Androgyns and Deviants - Industrial Romance for Bruised and Battered Angels, 1992–1995
description: A new compilation looks back on the storied New York drag ensemble where ANOHNI got her start, placing the troupe in a lineage of queer artists who treated drag as a means of accessing selfhood.

title: Sunrise Bang Ur Head Against tha Wall EP
description: On her second solo EP in two years, the rising UK producer leans into her fusion of jungle breaks and irresistible melodies. Her emotional acuity reveals the makings of a uniquely talented pop writer.

title: The Ceiling Reposes
description: The Chicago cellist duets with scraps of radio and field recordings on her bold and strangely moving second record.

title: Notorious Dump Legends: Volume 2
description: The rappers deliver an album filled with serpentine, enigmatic stories and gloomy beats. It doesn’t have the gloss and pomp of their best work, but it highlights the pair’s complementary gifts.

title: Milk for Flowers
description: The Welsh songwriter’s fifth album flits between whimsical psych-pop levity and candid expressions of grief. At its best, it brings the two together.

title: UK GRIM
description: It’s the irascible British duo’s most varied album to date. Just don’t expect anything to change.

title: Godcaster
description: The Brooklyn art-rock band continues to be proudly over the top on its relentless and theatrical second album.

title: Music
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Madonna’s first album of the new millennium, a maximalist dance-pop experiment that made the people come together.

title: Gemini Girl: The Complete Hush Recordings
description: Collected on a new anthology, the two albums from the supple-voiced ’70s singer-songwriter mine the internal turmoil of coming of age.

title: Radical Romantics
description: Karin Dreijer’s richly detailed third album renders the search for love as something both sensual and alien.

title: A View of a Landscape
description: L’Rain, Jlin, Kelsey Lu, Jason Moran, and more join the sculptor and sound artist for a meditation on the complex histories evoked by the antique cotton gin at the center of his 2018 Whitney Museum exhibition.

title: Rotten Bun for an Eggless Century
description: On her debut solo album, the Dama Scout singer explores her heritage and grapples with otherness in knotty electro-pop shot through with field recordings and traditional Chinese instruments.

title: Elegies for the Drift
description: The former Megafaun drummer uses a resonant, melodic palette of gamelan, thumb piano, and metallophones to achieve gemlike tones and ambient atmospheres.

title: Ben
description: Macklemore’s earnest yet clunky new album attempts to split the difference between high-budget stadium pop and grimy boom-bap.

title: Gumbo
description: The East Atlanta rapper’s latest project is full of whimsical beats and DatPiff-era nostalgia. It proves you don’t need shiny pop hooks to make a thrilling rap record in 2023.

title: Kyiv Eternal
description: The Ukrainian electronic musician collages a decade of field recordings into a moving tribute to the resilience of his hometown in wartime.

title: Ugly
description: The British rapper’s third album is likely to be his most polarizing: He trades rapping and electronic beats for ballads and rage rock. The results are largely underwhelming.

title: Somebody’s Child
description: On his most substantial solo release to date, the longstanding club MC slots into Manchester’s rich lineage of maverick dance musicians.

title: I Play My Bass Loud
description: The debut solo album from the Raincoats bassist is adventurous and collaborative and vibrant and furious.

title: The Songs of Bacharach & Costello (Super Deluxe)
description: Centered on 1998’s timeless Painted From Memory, this new compilation showcases the songwriters’ unlikely collaboration and the malleable and enduring songs that emerged from it.

title: Aurora
description: The soundtrack for a new Amazon Original series seeks to emulate the magic of Fleetwood Mac. More often than not, it ends up sounding like a Broadway tribute.

title: Food Near Me, Weather Tomorrow
description: The Rhode Island trio’s weirdo avant-pop tunes land somewhere between the subversive, no-wave skronk of Bush Tetras and the lo-fi minimalism of Sneaks.

title: Extreme Fantasy
description: The Philadelphia-based artist uses damaged acoustic guitars, piercing electronics, and unsettling vocals to construct a grotesque and hermetic world, conjuring visions of abject terror.

title: WOW
description: The Russian electronic musician’s latest album turns pointillist quirks into erratic maximalism—call it pop music for people who enjoy both Karlheinz Stockhausen and Lisa Frank.

title: Thanks 4 Nothing
description: Though a couple of safe songs threaten to slow the momentum, the Chicago artist sounds more defiant and grounded than ever on her fourth album.

title: Cluster I
description: The debut album from the duo of John Talabot and fellow Barcelona producer Velmondo spins a shadowy, subterranean web.

title: Feeling Body
description: On her debut album, the Kenyan composer folds field recordings, ambient textures, and layered vocalizations into a gripping meditation on illness and healing.

title: The Gold Experience
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Prince’s best album of the ’90s, a funked-out opus mired in extra-musical drama.

title: Soul’d Out: The Complete Wattstax Collection
description: Stax Records’ historic 1972 soul festival finally gets its due with a new 12-disc box set, presenting a pop label at its imperial peak and an unmediated vision of Blackness for a rapt audience.

title: Red Moon in Venus
description: On her lush and captivating third album, the pop star looks to the heavens, summoning the cosmic power of love and the divine feminine.

title: One Thing at a Time
description: Modern country’s prodigal son returns with a 36-song album that says a whole lot of nothing.

title: Another Planet 4
description: The New York rappers’ complementary styles unlock a world of imagistic detail and surreal coincidence.

title: Goodnight Neanderthal
description: On his second album, the Sydney punk fleshes out his filthy bubblegum scuzz with riffs, jokes, the requisite car song, and even a few unexpectedly vulnerable moments.

title: Dogsbody
description: On its debut album, the New York band’s expertly contained noise-rock din is the perfect foil to frontman Cole Haden’s white-hot charisma.

title: Amar
description: Though it sometimes follows rags-to-riches templates a little too closely, the Texas rapper’s debut is a compelling blend of theater and technical intricacy.

title: I Don’t Wanna Be Too Cool (Expanded Edition)
description: Captured Tracks issues an expanded LP version of songwriter Kate Fagan’s 1981 single, a cheeky rejoinder to consumerist status-seeking that became a DIY hit.

title: Cookup
description: The ambient-jazz saxophonist offers unpredictable, impressionistic takes on R&B hits from the ’90s and early ’00s, tackling songs by Beyoncé, Aaliyah, and Erykah Badu.

title: 7s
description: Rooted in demos made early in the pandemic, Avey Tare’s fourth solo album is unusual and slightly disarming: a head-over-heels-in-love album that’s also prickly and claustrophobic.

title: Strange Dance
description: The Radiohead drummer returns with a solo album whose beautiful, dramatic arrangements clash with the bland songwriting.

title: Burnin’ (Expanded Edition)
description: Featuring his eternal hit “Boom Boom,” the blues legend’s 1962 classic gets an anniversary reissue that showcases how rock’n’roll took shape around his timeless, elemental boogie.

title: Even God Has a Sense of Humor
description: The California rapper takes stock of his life on an introspective album that balances melancholy and bliss over lush, sampled loops and opulent live-band instrumentation.

title: 19 Naughty III (30th Anniversary)
description: When hip-hop was split between being an industry force or a niche subculture, the New Jersey trio’s second album proved they could bridge the gap between commercial success and artistic credibility.

title: Good Riddance
description: The artist’s full-length debut is an honest step forward, but emotional vulnerability can’t save it from the clichés of confessional songwriting.

title: flounder
description: The New Jersey indie-folk singer’s debut is a refreshingly modern take on classic themes of displacement, devolution, and love, of course.

title: Bless This Mess
description: Meg Remy’s most free-ranging and least narrative-minded album draws on retro funk and ’80s R&B as it infuses her biting social critique and wry humor with fresh optimism.

title: Shook
description: With a crew of equally radical peers in tow, the Atlanta band’s new album is a dissonant but hopeful statement about dreaming up a better world.
These unearthed recordings of an early solo piano performance showcase the composer’s ecstatic approach to melody and repetition.

title: Anthronomicon / Helionomicon
description: The death-metal trio is at its most complex on this pair of companion albums. Beneath the labyrinthine riffs lies some of the group’s sharpest, most distinctive music yet.

title: The Future
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Leonard Cohen at the end of history, wielding the darkest, glossiest, most bizarrely righteous songs of his career.

title: Should’ve Learned by Now
description: The Memphis alt-country lifers return with an endearing and impassioned album about drinking and the many reasons we do it.

title: Food for Worms
description: The British rockers’ third album peels away from the talky post-punk pack, emphasizing melody, ramshackle piano, and reflections on friendship.

title: Workin’ on a World
description: On her first collection of original material in over a decade, the country-folk songwriter frames observations of modern life in timeless American musical forms.

title: Practice
description: Sofia Jensen’s gentle indie-folk debut is a portrait of growing up with soul-baring lyrics and occasional breakthroughs.

title: Mind Palace Music
description: The Philadelphia/Baltimore duo recorded their 2021 debut remotely from their respective bedrooms, but the album—newly reissued by Carpark—captures the spirit of folk-pop at its most intimate.

title: Cracker Island
description: Stevie Nicks, Thundercat, Tame Impala, and Bad Bunny guest on the latest album from Damon Albarn’s cartoon band, but despite the marquee names, the record feels frustratingly like Gorillaz as usual.

title: Mourning Due
description: The hushed flows from the Brooklyn-based rapper are compelling, but some of her stories struggle to captivate.

title: Desire Pathway
description: The New Jersey band turns in another solid album of old-school riffs and ripping solos, but the songs stop just short of the radio-rock anthems they want to become.

title: Quest for Fire / Don’t Get Too Close
description: The dubstep disruptor returns with two albums—one of super-massive bass juggernauts, one of dizzy emo-rap—that make a surprisingly strong case for the Skrillex reboot.

title: Our Likeness
description: On her 1992 album, the iconoclastic vocalist and her band of German experimentalists pushed each other to virtuosic extremes, spanning styles and genres.

title: The Corner: Vol. 1
description: With terse existential inquiries and sun-faded samples, the full-length collaboration between the London rapper and the Brooklyn producer sounds at home on two continents.

title: extra life EP
description: On its debut EP, the Los Angeles duo pulls from favorite sounds of the 1990s to create effortless, widescreen dream pop that’s serene without being sentimental.

title: Release Spirit
description: On a lively new album, the electronic producer is a master of atmosphere, creating a mood of childlike whimsy while teasing a future in dream-pop songwriting.

title: 夢之駭客 Dream Hacker
description: Singing in English and Mandarin, the Berklee-educated vocalist and experimental musician uses oddball pop melodies, distorted breaks, and swirling drones to explore themes of anxiety and selfhood.

title: Like Dying Stars, We’re Reaching Out
description: Noah Weinman’s cloudy, spacious indie folk songs ruminate on the limits of human communication.

title: GLOW
description: The British singer, rapper, and producer’s second project approaches the challenge of self-discovery through graceful avant-R&B.

title: Season of Glass
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the first album Yoko Ono recorded after the death of her husband, a brittle and gorgeous capsule of hope triumphing over grief.

title: Transmissions From Total Refreshment Centre
description: Produced in collaboration with Blue Note, a new collection documents some of the artists and sounds emanating from the London cultural institution at the epicenter of contemporary jazz.

title: All Fiction
description: On their latest album, the Boston trio explores an eerie, percussion-heavy sound that maintains the adventurous spirit of their best work.

title: Anevite Void
description: More science than fiction, Detroit techno maven Erika Sherman’s lean and icy new album plugs into the subtle environmental flux of an alien planet.

title: The Land, the Water, the Sky
description: Katherine Paul’s third album of patient, cinematic indie rock surveys a return trip to her ancestral lands in the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community—and the hard-won peace she found once she arrived.

title: Dust Gatherers
description: On her first solo album in over a decade, the avant-pop artist weaves introspective thoughts through shapeshifting, operatic arrangements.

title: lil spirits
description: The UK mystery duo’s new EP is a more playful affair than Icons, more explicit in its internet-brained aesthetics—yet a little less exciting, too.

artist: Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs Pigs
title: Land of Sleeper
description: The UK quintet has a blast playing old-school stoner metal, balancing the riffs with sharp songwriting and a touch of camp.

title: Maritz
description: On a charming new solo album, the HTRK vocalist writes lighthearted folk music about loss and longing.

title: Girl in the Half Pearl
description: Liv.e’s brilliant second album bends her expressive R&B into fearsome new shapes, acknowledging all the nuance and pain on the long journey to personal truth.

title: Audiodidactic
description: Seven years after his debut, the Top Dawg fixture returns to his habitual stylistic fusions but too often, his muddy, psychedelic haze fails to summon the dreamlike quality it’s aiming for.

title: Sugar World
description: The Swedish artist better known as Yung Lean makes an unexpected pivot on his long-running side project, swapping out sad rap and vaporwave to embrace his inner crooner.

title: Desire, I Want to Turn Into You
description: Caroline Polachek’s best album of her career is a transformative pop experience, a passionate, richly melodic odyssey into the darkest corners of love.

title: Norm
description: The Canadian musician’s latest album is his most ambitious yet: a lush, cryptic, and creepy suite that questions the very concept of love.

title: Breaking the Balls of History
description: After a decade, Janet Weiss and Sam Coomes’ band returns with an album that’s musically rejuvenated but lyrically nearsighted.

title: Moments of Clarity
description: The Houston rock band’s third album captures a certain kind of painful, melodic bliss that comes in the wake of a crisis.

title: Raven
description: Kelela’s rapturous second album is a masterful display of tension and release, centering queer Black womanhood through blasts of heated dance music and ambient comedowns.

title: Let Her Burn
description: To shed the stigma of “Friday,” Rebecca Black reinvents herself as a desperate hyperpop star.

title: Pollen
description: Much as it always has, the married duo’s confectionary indie pop lands somewhere between pleasantly forgettable, reliably vibey, and genuinely inspiring.

title: He Left Nothing for the Swim Back
description: On his full-length Backwoodz debut, SKECH185’s hoarsely confrontational rapping finds a perfect match in producer Jeff Markey’s jumpy, abrasive beats.

title: Complex Simplicity
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Teedra Moses’ silken debut, a cult classic of 2000s R&B.

title: Segue to Infinity
description: The Numero release includes some of Laraaji’s breathtaking, newly discovered zither and kalimba odysseys. It reaffirms his preeminent role in ambient history.

title: This Is Why
description: Hayley Williams and co. pivot to jittery, crackling post-punk on their sixth album, but the monotone vocals and political lyrics don’t always play to their strengths.

title: War Lord
description: With shades of late-’90s New Orleans and mid-aughts trap, the Detroit rapper’s newest mixtape casts an ominous spell even when his writing isn’t at its strongest.

title: Oh Glistening Onion, the Nighttime Is Coming
description: On her debut album, the Brooklyn folk singer writes vividly detailed songs about the peculiarities of human emotion, turning existential questions into playful country romps and homey campfire songs.

title: This Stupid World
description: On their liveliest album in at least a decade, indie rock’s most steadfast institution squares up against ubiquitous darkness.

title: Anarchist Gospel
description: The Los Angeles folk-punk singer-songwriter steps into a more expansive, considered sound, blending various strains of American roots music into a quietly idiosyncratic style.

title: Today My Friend You Drunk the Venom
description: The Cincinnati post-punks craft melodic, hard-driving pop in service of eerie, unsolvable riddles.

title: My 21st Century Blues
description: The UK pop upcomer put her former record label on blast, then scored her first No. 1 hit. Her debut full-length makes an ambitious but uneven bid for independent stardom.

title: The Candle and the Flame
description: Accompanied by family members and former bandmates, the Go-Betweens songwriter crafts a sparse but deeply felt album.

title: Colours of Air
description: Two artists from opposite sides of the ambient spectrum find common cause in a 132-year-old pipe organ.

title: Petals EP
description: On his debut EP for Hessle Audio, the Jordanian producer brings regional rhythms and Arabic maqam scales to cutting-edge club music.

title: Rush!
description: The Italian rock band has become a global sensation. Their new album is absolutely terrible at every conceivable level.

title: Heavy Heavy
description: Defined by small acts of joyful resistance, the Edinburgh group’s fourth album is a celebration of music as shared and spontaneous practice.

title: University!
description: Full of plinking synths, blown-out bass, and skittering beats, the Atlanta producer’s latest compilation sounds like the flyest rap video game never made.

title: Smalltown Stardust
description: Steeped in the warm, psychedelic pop-rock of the 1970s, the new record from erstwhile garage rocker Kyle Thomas is a gold-toned nostalgia voyage that’s never entirely familiar.

title: New York City
description: The Brooklyn band’s ninth album is an unpretentious garage-punk racket that wears its analog heart on flannel-clad sleeves.

title: The Waeve
description: Combining modular synth, saxophone, and a medieval lute, Graham Coxon and Rose Elinor Dougall create an album of pastoral disquiet and itchy post-punk edge.

title: The Abyssal Plain
description: The Iowa black metal quartet’s debut explores the mystery of the deep seas with shapeshifting, dynamic songwriting.

title: workshop 32
description: German deep-house technician Gunnar Wendel’s new album for the Workshop label clears away the murk of his early work, achieving disorienting effects with its oddly pristine palette.

title: Anthology of American Folk Music, Vol. 1-3
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Harry Smith’s foundational 1952 mixtape that used the United States’ rich musical inheritance to suggest how we might better ourselves

title: Great Is He
description: Trite where it should be subtle and mellow where it should be exciting, the Jamaican star’s new album fails to consistently capture his magic.

title: Queen of Me
description: Working with a team of hit-making collaborators, the country-pop icon returns with a bland collection of optimistic affirmations and pumping electro-pop rhythms.

title: Chess Moves
description: The underground hip-hop veteran’s new EP flirts with chess metaphors, but the mundane raps don’t help the thematic wallpaper hold up.

title: Portrait of a Dog
description: Produced by BADBADNOTGOOD, the second album from the Hiroshima-born, Montreal-based singer-songwriter explores heartbreak and familial history with a subtle and dynamic approach.

title: Love Is War
description: The North Carolina rapper refines his technical wizardry on his second album, but he’s too often buried by 9th Wonder and Khrysis’ overblown production.

title: After the Magic
description: On the South Korean artist’s astounding third album, the past and the present, the real and the fake dissolve seamlessly into surreal, maximalist pop music.

title: Living
description: The London singer-songwriter’s debut LP frames big themes—the heaviness of life and death, the duality in ecstasy and pain—in skeletal, atmospheric indie rock.

title: Wendy
description: On his new album, the Nicolás Jaar collaborator undergoes a vivid technicolor upgrade but his songwriting doesn’t always leave an impression.

title: Let’s Start Here.
description: Despite its intriguing concept, Lil Yachty’s voyage into soul and psych-rock runs aground.

title: Furling
description: Largely centered on the piano, the songwriter’s first solo album in eight years is wistful, heady, and mesmerizing.

title: Dead Meat
description: Former Joanna Gruesome guitarist Owen “O” Williams’ new group taps into the chiming sound of ’80s college rock, channeling a wide range of jangly inspirations.

title: Blue Period
description: A remastered double-LP compilation of the D.C. art-punks’ early 2000s material showcases their atmospheric, Wurtlitzer-haloed approach to indie rock.

title: Every Acre
description: Tranquil and reverberant, the North Carolina folk songwriter’s new album finds relief and resolution in the circadian rhythms of the natural world.

title: AudioLust & HigherLove
description: The second album from the UK pop producer is pleasant and anonymous, all good vibes and cabana jams.

title: Letters to George
description: Featuring dual saxophones, synthesizers, voice, and drums, the new group led by Montreal composer John Hollenbeck analyzes pop songcraft through a jazz lens.

title: We Cater to Cowards
description: The Chicago headbangers’ fifth LP is a confident nod to early grunge. It’s an unusually succinct statement for them, with leaner songwriting and more pointed barbs.

title: Fragments - Time Out of Mind Sessions (1996-1997): The Bootleg Series, Vol. 17
description: Spanning the sessions for 1997’s Time Out of Mind, an illuminating new edition of Bob Dylan’s Bootleg Series both subverts and magnifies the legend of his haunted, trancelike comeback album.

title: Honey
description: After an arresting opener, the singer-songwriter’s second album wanders into a fog of existential angst and you-had-to-be-there anecdotes.

title: One Day
description: With anthemic hardcore hooks and unabashed lyrics about the power of love, the Toronto band’s latest album radiates fired-up joy.

title: Fatima
description: A psychogeographic survey of the Himalayan region of Ladakh rendered in ambient drones and harsh noise, Fatima doubles as an uneasy chronicle of capitalist exploitation and generational trauma.

title: Stillmatic
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 2001 resurrection of Nas, a canonical comeback album that came out swinging and never backed down.

title: Gloria
description: Sam Smith remains a bit of a pop paradox, a trailblazing figure who often settles into well-trodden songwriting.

title: Asking for a Ride
description: The Louisville rock band refines its major-label sound on a brief but charming new album: It hits hardest when you don’t think too much about it.

title: Lobes
description: Steeped in ’80s revivalism, the New York dance-rockers’ eighth album is a hazy tapestry of half-remembered sounds and shopworn tropes.

title: Before the Gloss Up
description: In spite of a few obligatory major label maneuvers, the Memphis rapper’s debut mixtape preserves her charisma with a rush of shit-talking and warning shots.

title: To What End
description: On his 10th solo studio album, the Brooklyn-based underground rap vet unpacks emotional baggage and asks what—if anything—he’s willing to compromise for the sake of success.

title: Graffiti in Space
description: Turning his ear for imperfection toward dub techno, versatile producer Paul Dickow turns out six tracks that conceal worlds of activity under their grimy patina.

title: Does Spring Hide Its Joy
description: Presented as a sprawling three-hour epic, the composer’s drone piece for guitar, cello, and sine wave oscillators seeks new rhythms within the interminable sweep of pandemic time.

title: Ace (50th Anniversary Deluxe Edition)
description: Featuring multiple songs that became staples of the Grateful Dead’s live set, the 1972 solo debut by the guitarist and singer gets a deluxe edition with a new mix and some recent live recordings.

title: Rap Game Awful
description: The rising road-rap talent has built his name on a mixture of sinister detachment and bristling ambition. Yet despite his aloof, exacting style, he stretches himself thin on this 28-track mixtape.

title: Mercy
description: On an often chilly album full of unexpected collaborations and smeared with apocalyptic terror, the 80-year-old art-rock legend grapples with the need for human connection.

title: Surgery Channel
description: Ty and Denée Segall, along with the Cairo Gang’s Emmett Kelly, refine their abrasive sound on a record that writhes, swells, and undulates like the belly of a serpent.

title: Drifting
description: With pianist Johan Lindvall and cellist Judith Hamann, saxophonist and composer Mette Henriette presents hushed, repetitive meditations unbounded by the pressures of time.

title: Like..? EP
description: The crown princess of Bronx drill arrives with a down-to-earth attitude and a diabolical knack for hooks. Assume her naïveté at your own peril.

title: Time’s Arrow
description: On its seventh album, the Liverpool electro-pop band reaches for a lighter sound, capturing the passage of time in effervescent synths and impressionistic lyrics.

title: Saccades
description: Propulsive and winding, this collaborative album is a hypnotic exercise in reimagining the past and future of a Ugandan tradition.

title: Impossible Princess
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the Australian superstar’s 1997 departure to clubland, a misunderstood journey of self-discovery that became the black sheep of her catalog.

title: Five Easy Hot Dogs
description: A listless album about being listless, Mac DeMarco’s new collection of instrumentals summons the bleary, exhausted feeling of time spent on the road.

title: Bin Reaper 3: New Testament
description: On the fourth tape in his Bin Reaper series, the Michigan breakout looks to level up with slicker beats and bigger cosigns. Fortunately, he’s still rapping about NBA stars and SpongeBob.

title: Cyclamen
description: The Irish-Catalan singer-songwriter’s latest release is playful and elliptical, as reverent of folk-pop as it is invested in experimenting with it.

title: The Predator Nominate EP
description: A set of previously unreleased demos for the influential Dayton band’s never-completed major label debut offers a fascinating glimpse into their strange, singular evolution.

title: Cr​é​puscule I & II
description: Intimate yet cinematic, the Japanese musician’s new two-part album exchanges her colorful pop patchwork for soft, luminous ambient music of alien beauty and human warmth.

title: Aftersun (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
description: The composer and cellist’s score for Charlotte Wells’ film is full of suggestion and shadows, wringing emotion from the lightest touches.

title: A Short Diary
description: On a set inspired by his father’s death, jazz drummer Sebastian Rochford enlists pianist Kit Downes, a longtime collaborator, to help him tell a story about company and grief.

title: Free 03
description: On a new tape marking his release from prison, the Los Angeles rapper and folk hero sounds battered but resilient, mixing studio sessions with tracks recorded over the phone from inside.

title: Oh No EP
description: Drawing from footwork, jungle, acid, and more, the UK producer lets his breakneck tempos lead him to some of his funkiest, most kinetic—and oddly beautiful—work to date.

title: Songs for the Willow EP
description: The Wilkes-Barre hardcore band blends singalong accessibility, purgative heaviness, and thoughtful craft into songs about the disconnect between dreams and reality.
In a dozen somber, elegiac pieces for piano and electronics recorded in the wake of a cancer diagnosis, the Japanese composer reckons with his own mortality.

title: La Sustancia X
description: The Puerto Rican rapper wields impeccable flows and pointed barbs into a forceful statement of queer Caribbean spirit.

title: Prize
description: Working with minimalist guitar, gentle vocals, and an understated rhythm section, the English musician constructs a careful lesson about the awe of being present.

title: Monsters of Rap
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit a tacky, mail-order compilation that strangely, almost perfectly encapsulates the class of early-’90s pop-rap.

title: Late Developers
description: On the quick follow-up to last year’s A Bit of Previous, the Glasgow indie-pop band’s on-the-fly energy and head-in-the-clouds musings collide in memorable and surprising ways.

title: Strays
description: Embracing cosmic empathy and some welcome collaborations, the Nashville songwriter’s fourth album bursts with easy confidence and kind, stoic wisdom.

title: Sorry 4 Da Ooze
description: Surfing between piano-driven minimalism and hazy synth experiments, the Maryland rapper’s latest mixtape seeks the next evolution of DMV rap.

title: Every Loser
description: Working with pop architect Andrew Watt, the agelessly incendiary rocker unfurls a parade of timeless archetypes: profane punk, seedy crooner, lovable curmudgeon. It’s Iggy Pop as a jukebox musical.

title: Afrikantis
description: This is Lil B’s most head-turning proposition in years: an avant-garde electro-jazz album seemingly recorded with the cheapest MIDI presets on the market.

title: Sauce Ghetto Gospel 3
description: The Houston rapper reprises his Sauce Ghetto Gospel series, bringing his booming baritone to diaristic confessions and slick songs of celebration.

title: SNOOP CUBE 40 $HORT
description: Jumping from the blockchain to streaming platforms, the four West Coast OGs offer an album’s worth of trunk-rattling traditionalism that celebrates their exalted elder status.

title: The Work
description: After six years, Derwin Dicker returns to his primary project for a lush, sun-drenched set with a genuine emotional charge.

title: NADAWORLD 2
description: With adrenaline, heart, and an unmistakable Baltimore accent, Deetranada breathes fresh life into the familiar struggles of the up-and-coming rapper.

title: Landwerk No. 3
description: On the third album in his series based on loops of early 20th-century, mostly Yiddish records, the guitarist and archivist incorporates more instrumentation and more space.

title: Trillstatik 2
description: Written and recorded in a guest-filled marathon session, the Texas legend’s second live outing with producer Statik Selektah carries a spirit of friendly competition.

title: The Water Is the Shovel of the Shore
description: Laying bare the strangeness of their repertoire while connecting centuries-old songs to modern struggles, the London collective approaches folk song as a living tradition, not a museum piece.

title: Ultratronics
