description: The pop star’s first live album is a collage of Miley’s various eras and personas, not all of which have aged well or translate coherently to a live setting.

title: Ramona Park Broke My Heart
description: The companion piece to his 2021 self-titled record diverges from the innovation and technical proficiency in favor of introspection and contemplation. It is a richly detailed, deadpan elegy for his stolen youth.

title: Familia
description: Camila Cabello’s third album embarks on an exploration of her musical heritage while holding onto familiar themes of love and anxiety. She swings big and often hits.

title: Trendsetter
description: The New Jersey rapper and singer’s full-length debut is wide-ranging and unfocused—but it never lacks for energy.

title: B.I.B.L.E.
description: The Brooklyn rapper’s official debut is focused on creating the type of inoffensive watered-down drill that would make a certain mayor happy.

title: The Line Is a Curve
description: The London-based literary polymath’s fourth album fuses spoken-word poetry with skeletal production, painting a picture of contemporary UK culture in imagistic, intricately wrought verse.

title: Live at Shea Stadium
description: This 2015 live set at the Brooklyn all-ages venue captures Conor Oberst’s reunited punk band digging into its scrappy, DIY roots.

title: Together
description: The trio’s second album post-hiatus matches the clarity of its arrangements with an unexpected spiritual lightness. Rarely has Duster sounded so pleasant and peaceful.

title: Rave & Roses
description: On his promising debut, the Nigerian star has figured out exactly how he wants to sound, but he hasn’t quite nailed what he wants to say.

title: Broken Hearts Club
description: Syd reshapes heartbreak into pillowy, ’80s-nodding R&B on her second album, softening her sound while maintaining vulnerability in her songwriting.

title: Aethiopes
description: The rapper’s latest album is a clear mid-career apex that shoves his always outlandish style into territories further afield than ever before.

title: The Parts I Dread
description: Summoning the communal energy of a live band, the indie rock songwriter’s debut explores uneasy emotions, anxiety spirals, and perseverance.

title: Turn It On!
description: Led by charismatic vocalist Alanna Oliver, the Australian rock band draws on vintage references with enthusiasm and pomp, shooting their songs into the stratosphere.

title: Warping All by Yourself
description: The latest from free-folk journeyman Matt Valentine delves into lysergic funk and psychedelic self-reflection.

title: At Fillmore East
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 1971 live double LP from the Allman Brothers Band, a snapshot of a pure and joyous moment in rock’n’roll.

title: Terror Twilight: Farewell Horizontal
description: Pavement’s swan song finally gets the full reissue treatment, with various demos, alternate versions, and a new track sequence. It remains a fascinatingly ambivalent note to finish on for one of the most influential indie rock bands of their era.

title: En Átomos Volando
description: Using corroded samples and languid tempos, Bogotá artist Nicolás Vallejo casts an eerie and sorrowful light on Colombia’s hidden traumas.

title: Chloë and the Next 20th Century
description: Singer-songwriter Josh Tillman reaches far, far back to the golden age of Hollywood for a dreamy, lushly orchestrated, wryly comic collection of vignettes that all depend upon the timelessness of a love song.

title: Bronco
description: Working with producer Jay Joyce and Nashville session musicians, the masked cult figure adopts the widescreen scale of mainstream country while stretching his eccentricities to their limits.

title: Picnic in the Dark
description: Having traded city life for the Catskills, the New York artist explores a more relaxed sound on the follow-up to 2018’s Old Ghost, finding new purpose in her soft-focus optimism.

title: Wet Leg
description: The British indie rock duo have hooks stuffed with bait and a keen eye for assessing self-delusion. Their debut is the sound of two women stoking mutiny from a slow descent into madness.

title: You Belong There
description: With intricate guitar playing, vulnerable songwriting, and a surprising turn toward free-jazz exploration, the Grizzly Bear multi-instrumentalist reintroduces himself on his full-length solo debut.

title: Fear of the Dawn
description: On his first of two solo albums planned for this year, Jack White earns his eccentricity. An illogical fusion of blues-rock and carnival prog, this music is genuinely, imaginatively weird.

title: Cash Romantic
description: Tom and Ed Russell continue to test various hybrids of techno, UK garage, and for the first time, drum’n’bass, but the EP’s most promising moment looks beyond the dancefloor.

title: Growing Up
description: On their debut album, the teen (and pre-teen) punk rockers turn adolescent angst and razor-sharp hooks into heartwarming pop-punk with ample charm.

title: Tuqoos
description: The Ramallah producer-rapper’s debut is a border-agnostic collection of beats that participates in a global dialogue while retaining a distinctly Palestinian identity.
The Atlanta rapper’s second album asserts her confidence and versatility, rounding out the trap beats with tracks that draw on pop, gospel, and R&B sounds.

title: Oneiric
description: The Austin experimental musician’s grand, romantic ambient album is inspired by dreams’ blissful connotations and cryptic communications.

title: Leave the Light On
description: The Dublin rock quartet’s second album considers the toll of living up to expectations—romantic, platonic, and societal—with a new gravitas that smothers some of the band’s fire.

title: Parrhesia
description: On their third album as a trio, the prog metal band refines their interplay and finds a sweet spot between technical precision and human flourish.

title: Quitters
description: With help from Phoebe Bridgers and Conor Oberst, the California songwriter tells conversational, painfully precise stories of sad sacks, lost souls, hopeless drunks, and ex-boyfriends.

title: Mr Mixondo
description: Though still suited for delirious outdoor parties, the 19-year-old Tanzanian musician’s take on singeli is as much about the spiritual connection between producer and laptop as it is the dancefloor.

title: I Just Want to Be a Good Man
description: The debut album from the late Oakland pastor is a powerful showcase for his guitar work, his singing, and his ministry.

title: Maida Vale Sessions / Microtronics / Mother Is the Milky Way
description: Three rarities collections by the pioneering English band offer a small survey of their evolution from a conventional pop outfit to psych visionaries.

title: I Don’t Like You
description: On his proper debut, the 24-year-old artist dabbles in generic singer-songwriter pastiche, flattening what made his intimate, solitary music so promising in the first place.

title: THE UNRAVELING OF PUPTHEBAND
description: The Toronto band returns with a supremely hooky, slightly more polished album about harnessing dread to make music to harness dread to.

title: The ReVe Festival 2022 - Feel My Rhythm
description: On a new mini-album, the K-pop group known for bold summer hits returns with refined, verdant dance-pop better suited for springtime.

title: The Specials
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 1979 debut from the rambunctious and politically charged UK group the Specials, a marquee document of the ska revival.

title: Mainstream Sellout
description: The enfant terrible of the pop-rock revival wades deeper into the genre, coming back with even less than before.

title: Gold - Go Forward in the Courage of Your Love
description: The Mancunian saxophonist and poet’s warm and wise album is a balm of spoken word and spiritual jazz, both strangely uncomfortable and strangely comforting.

title: Opening the Door
description: The Mood Hut co-founder’s full-length debut and first release in seven years is a lighthearted collection of deep house, dub, yacht rock, and ambient sketches.

title: Third Album
description: Thirteen years after their last album together, the electroclash icons return to their roots.

title: I Know NIGO!
description: The Japanese fashion designer’s passion project is characteristically stylish and star-studded, featuring contributions from Pharrell, Kanye West, Tyler the Creator, and the late Pop Smoke.

title: Country Coming Down
description: On his new set of late-night country disco, the Texas singer known as “Big Velvet” leans into the cartoonish undertones of his booming baritone. He always sounded oversized—now he makes music to match.

title: I Don’t Know My Words
description: The former Yeasayer member returns with a refreshingly uninhibited, occasionally undercooked set of 1970s-style singer-songwriter music.

title: Barbara
description: Brooklyn’s Barrie Lindsay makes lush, dance-inflected indie pop whose unorthodox influences and imaginative twists shine brighter than the lyrics.

title: Unlimited Love
description: After more than a decade away, guitarist John Frusciante returns for the band’s first album in six years, a restrained and familiar effort to recapture an old spark in a new era.

title: Us Ephemeral
description: The 100% Electronica affiliate channels bits of techo, trance, 2-step, and jungle into contemporary rave hybrids tempered with a hint of vaporwave’s self-awareness.

title: Interior Monologues
description: Mixing speech and singing, the New York-based sound poet and experimental musician meditates on meaning, context, and impermanence.

title: American Gurl
description: The shapeshifting multimedia artist ventures into pop with a concept album that stages arch critiques of art and consumerism within a retro arcade game.

title: Diaspora Problems
description: On their groundbreaking new album, the Philadelphia hardcore group mixes actionable rhetoric, absurdist humor, and breathtaking vulnerability like no band before them.

title: Get Wet.Radio
description: With a newfound penchant for slow jams, the Detroit rapper’s latest emphasizes his emotional depth, cartoonish humor, and attention to detail.

title: Running With the Hurricane
description: Shifting away from the gnawing, emo-inflected power-pop of their first two albums, the Melbourne trio ask: Can softness be as invigorating as fury?

title: In February
description: Combining synthesizers, field recordings, nylon-string guitar, and hushed singing, the Istanbul-born, Glasgow-based musician creates an intimate take on laptop folk.

title: Gifted
description: Breezy, uplifting, and never forced, the Jamaican reggae star’s debut imbues the ennui and uncertainty of this epoch with much-needed positivity.

title: SZNZ: Spring
description: Rivers Cuomo toys with Renaissance Faire shtick on the first of four planned EPs inspired by Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons.

title: New Preoccupations
description: The Philly band takes influence from the earnest, unfashionable alt-rock of the 1990s on a moving set about sobriety and freedom.

title: Melt My Eyez See Your Future
description: The South Florida rapper internalizes his skeptical gaze, yielding music that’s more deliberately self-reflective, with few ragers or bangers.

title: Famously Alive
description: The trio’s latest is a beautiful mess of squelchy psych-pop—emphasis on pop—where effervescent instrumentals soundtrack an earnest and hard-earned lust for life.

title: Candydrip
description: The New Orleans singer’s lush, sultry soul-pop goes down almost too easy.

title: Maxinquaye
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the Massive Attack associate’s 1995 debut, a gloomy unicorn of contemporary UK pop.

title: Humble Quest
description: The Nashville songwriter returns with a comfortable set of country-pop, colored by grief and new motherhood. It feels matter-of-factly masterful.

title: Warm Chris
description: The New Zealand songwriter returns with a sparse and oblique album whose gentle psychedelic folk and beguiling free association proudly resist interpretation.

title: Nightclub Daydreaming
description: On the Baltimore duo’s fourth album, Ed Schrader and Devlin Rice trade their formerly frenetic energy for ’80s sounds and danceable beats.

title: Electricity
description: The London-based ensemble taps Hot Chip to flesh out the dimensions of its cosmopolitan blend of West African funk and electronic bass music.

title: Recordings From the Åland Islands
description: With trickles of piano, synth, and viola, the Los Angeles-based collaborators shape a tranquil vision of a Nordic landscape that feels just beyond the edge of reality.

title: The Bear
description: On a bittersweet and impressionistic solo album, the former Walkmen member confronts the joys and humiliations of a life devoted to music.

title: Adolescence
description: Pushing beyond his playlist origins, the New Zealand producer’s debut album revels in eccentric details while adhering to traditional pop structures.

title: Labyrinthitis
description: Dan Bejar’s marvelously inscrutable songwriting reaches beyond meaning. On his most live-sounding record in years, he finds clarity when language recedes and the music takes over.

title: In/Out/In
description: On these five mostly instrumental recordings from between 2000 and 2010, Sonic Youth dig in and stretch out.

title: Weavings
description: Nicolás Jaar’s collaborative project for the 2020 Unsound Festival gathers Angel Bat Dawid, Laraaji, Senyawa, and a dozen more artists in a pensive, shapeshifting piece of pandemic-era live improvisation.

title: Crest
description: The Drain Gang collaboration is one of the best projects to come out of the rap and hyperpop-adjacent Swedish collective. It’s a softly textured and sweetly spiritual quest for something bigger than ourselves.

title: In Dimes We Trust
description: The San Antonio-based rapper rides menacing, three-dimensional beats with steely confidence and creative flows, but he’s most interesting as a storyteller.

title: Forever
description: The posthumous Phife Dawg album, a showcase for his dexterous vocal style, reveals what had become most important to the rapper’s life in his post-Tribe years.

title: Kongestion
description: The Swedish duo continues to find new ways of mangling techno’s lexicon.

title: GrindHard E vs. YSR Gramz
description: Styled like a boxing match until they get bored with the concept and abandon it, the raucous mixtape still proves Flint, Michigan has another rap duo worth talking about.

title: a journey…
description: Using field recordings and modular synths, the UK-based electronic musician channels the holistic energies of forest bathing.

title: better luck next time. EP
description: The 18-year-old rapper continues to polish his frenetic breed of pop-trap while maintaining a fundamental weirdness that’s neither too loud nor too discreet.

title: Eat Your Food
description: Though the duo’s joint project feels tethered to tradition, there is something fairly radical about a pair of earnest rap nerds so devoted to the nuts and bolts.

title: Sore Thumb
description: The Long Island emo band’s adventurous new album is a document of abstract experiments and stoned afternoons, stranger than their previous work while still buzzing with the pursuit of bliss.

title: Plants Singing
description: On her debut album, the Newcastle-via-Melbourne songwriter works slowly and methodically, lamenting her past and praying for the future.

title: Alpha
description: Blending dancehall with pop-rap, 1980s soul, and 2000s R&B, the Jamaican singer’s full-length debut makes a flashy play for the mainstream.

title: Mowing the Leaves Instead of Piling ’Em Up
description: The Asheville indie-rock quintet delivers an album’s worth of covers, revealing their influences via songs by Drive-By Truckers, Smashing Pumpkins, and Roger Miller.

title: Kazemachi Roman
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit an overlooked masterpiece from 1971, one that helped define the essence of Japanese rock.

title: Are You Happy Now?
description: The singer-songwriter brings a more considered levity to her full-length debut, striking a balance between heartache and resolve.

title: a couple of good days
description: Playing fast and loose with his samples, the Austin, Texas, producer seems to ask: Why stick to any one genre or era when you can submit to the decadence of pure vibes?

title: Frank
description: On his proper debut album, the underground Virginia rapper sounds both flashy and laconic, seeming at once like an everyman and cooler than you.

title: It Was a Home
description: On her soulful second album, Chicago singer-songwriter Kaina Castillo reconciles childhood memories and future dreams with the hard work of getting through today.

title: Motomami
description: The Spanish superstar’s third album is a showcase for Rosalía’s exceptional range. It aspires to stretch itself out across genres and play with form, and attains exactly what it sets out to achieve.

title: Skærgårdslyd
description: The Denmark-born, Sweden-based experimentalist works with humble, home-recorded materials, but the richly expressive dimensions of her 4-track creations transcend their threadbare origins.

title: Tana Talk 4
description: The Buffalo rapper digs deeper into his established lore, savoring his victories while further stewing in past regrets.

title: Crash
description: Charli’s best full-length project since Pop 2 is a canny embrace of modern and vintage pop styles by one of its most sincere students.

title: Dark Matters
description: On his third album, the former Speedy Ortiz guitarist continues to carve out space for Black perspectives in indie rock while expanding his musical range.

title: Occam XXV
description: Occam XXV sustains a single organ drone for nearly 45 minutes, tracing a long, gradual arc of fluttering harmonics and microtonal pulses, sounding as alien as the French composer’s synthesizer work.

title: Good and Green Again
description: The folk musician’s latest album is a bittersweet collection full of silence and space. Delivered with empathy, his historical subject matter feels rooted in the present.
Durk’s latest offers some of the best and most honest crooning bars over smooth piano lines, but the formula is starting to wear thin.

title: Kiren
description: Shimizu’s long career has encompassed jazz fusion, city pop, and the omnivorous experiments of his group Mariah. This unreleased 1984 album showcases his electronic work at its most experimental.

title: Broken Equipment
description: The Brooklyn punks remain focused on the ceaseless challenges of living in the big city, but their overdriven guitars no longer sound quite as bitter or fed up—particularly when they shift to love songs.

title: Hygiene
description: The latest album from the chameleonic hardcore band is filled with pithy one-liners and gigantic hooks. Mired in anxiety, this music builds intimacy from commiseration.

title: Zhigeist
description: The duo’s collaborative project feels like an interstellar jam session that doesn’t push either of them too far from their comfort zones.

title: Dream River
description: The Irish musician’s spacious, shapeshifting synth pop submerges acoustic strums and babbling streams into a tender exploration of life’s inherent chaos.

title: Oxy Music
description: The impish artist’s fourth record attempts all of the same tricks that made his music so compelling earlier in his career, but with far less success.

title: The Great Regression
description: The English punks’ debut is a rage-forward bulldozer of poetic wordplay and experimental hardcore.

title: Keep On With Falling
description: The English band’s first album in over 20 years lacks the fuel and fire to elevate it from a good Britpop record into a great Boo Radleys record.

title: Mark VI
description: Armed with a bag full of vintage mixtapes that he discovered in the trunk of a used car, the Toronto producer and U.S. Girls affiliate whips up a lo-fi tribute to ’80s house, techno, and electro.

title: Below the Heavens
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 2007 debut from the L.A. duo, an enchanting hip-hop classic with an almost mythological history.

title: The Bed Is in the Ocean
description: The latest entry in a vital reissue series from Numero Group lives at the nexus of the Boston jazz-rock band’s strange evolution. Their daring interplay sounds as if the songs are still being constructed as you listen.

title: Classic Objects
description: The Norwegian artist presents her most unified mind-body work to date, melody-filled art-pop that deals with the nature of self and the freedom of the unconscious.

title: Forbidden Feelingz
description: Running influences from classic jungle, reggae, and R&B through pop music’s pithy filter, the Manchester producer is extending UK hardcore’s legacy to a new generation.

title: peace places: kenyan memories
description: On her latest EP, the Kenyan composer explores concepts of home and memory through a series of melodic sound collages.

title: This World Is Going to Ruin You
description: The second album from the Boston hardcore group is a tentative push toward accessibility, exploding its sound in new directions while nodding to familiar touchstones.

title: Diplo
description: Having recently gone through his country, psychedelic pop, and even ambient phases, the omnivorous EDM DJ turns his attention to house music on his first solo full-length in 18 years.

title: To Live & Die in Space & Time
description: As gentle as cherry blossoms on a spring breeze, the Minnesota musicians’ lush compositions for saxophone, piano, and synthesizer convey a wealth of feeling.

title: Sonescent
description: Inspired by a stint in silent meditation, these two sidelong pieces attempt to wrest orchestral order from real-life chaos.

title: Trap Cake, Vol. 2
description: The Puerto Rican singer’s EP is a mix of robot soul and trap beats that sound like he’s just having fun making expensive-sounding records.

title: Sunk
description: A new EP of soft, slowcore music from Maya Bon and Ryan Albert arrives like a postscript, elaborating on past themes of grief and accountability with a darker scrawl.

artist: Ilhan Ersahin / Dave Harrington / Kenny Wollesen
title: Invite Your Eye
description: On their first album as a trio, these jazz-rooted musicians create a luxurious atmosphere drawing from funk, krautrock, and noirish electronica.

title: Hunter on the Wing
description: A member of Trouble Books, Aqueduct Ensemble, and Lemon Quartet, Akron’s Keith Freund combines found sounds, acoustic instruments, and wonky electronics into evocative ambient miniatures.

title: Multitude
description: With biting humor and striking intimacy, the Belgian pop singer’s adventurous third album examines how we humans care for one another—or don’t.

title: Things Are Great
description: Band of Horses’ sixth album unexpectedly delivers on all the qualities that defined their initial success: soaring emotions, crunchy guitars, and Ben Bridwell’s cotton-candy whine.

title: Topical Dancer
description: The Belgian duo’s debut album pairs punchy, propulsive electro pop with inventive sound design, absurdist wit, and sly jabs at racism and xenophobia.

title: Growthfully Developed
description: Crack’s latest album is a delicate balance of fresh and familiar from one of the funniest and most thoughtful rappers working today.

title: Squeeze
description: Sasami Ashworth’s second solo album cleaves together two distinctively 1990s sound worlds as it asks: Can a song ever make it all the way to another person?

title: Duality
description: Early in the pandemic, the Toronto multi-instrumentalist’s bedroom videos made her a viral sensation. Now, her debut album puts a widescreen spin on those whimsical miniatures.

title: Once Upon a Time
description: The anonymous UK act construct a vast, vaporous tribute to the patron saint of love and heartbreak: Céline Dion.

title: Raum
description: On their second album since founding member Edgar Froese’s death in 2015, the German electronic maestros continue to supersize their signature brand of cosmic synth music.

title: How Is It That I Should Look at the Stars
description: Performed almost entirely at the piano, the follow-up to Tamara Lindeman’s 2021 breakthrough Ignorance raises dizzying questions with sensitivity and quiet hope.

title: Get Lifted
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 2004 debut from John Legend, one of hip-hop and R&B’s most soulful synergies.

title: Ocean Child: Songs of Yoko Ono
description: Curated by Ben Gibbard and featuring Sharon Van Etten, David Byrne, Japanese Breakfast and more, this tribute album fares best when the artists match Yoko Ono’s fearless spirit.

title: Love on My Mind
description: The Brooklyn post-punk band’s latest is a novella-like EP whose shoegaze blur and metallic twang animate a dreamlike world of seedy characters and half-forgotten pasts.

title: Ghetto Gods
description: On their latest album, the Atlanta duo paints a more intimate portrait of their city but struggles to personalize their homages. They hit their stride when they speak directly to the people.

title: There In Spirit
description: The Queens native brings a directness and precision to his latest album, an unassuming notebook of observations from a mature rapper with nothing left to prove.

title: PAINLESS
description: The singer-songwriter’s striking second album excels at a kind of subtle disclosure, relying less on power than it does texture and immaculately sparing detail.

title: Timewave Zero
description: The Denver death-metal quartet’s wordless, old-school, analog synth music flips the genre’s atmospheric interstitials into towering showstoppers that invite deep concentration.

title: Only Love From Now On
description: The experimental artist’s latest project is the most dynamic, unpredictable album of her career—a collection of instrumental music that flows like an interconnected suite.

title: Flute Music
description: On his 1977 solo debut, the American flutist probes the possibilities of his instrument: multi-tracking it, pairing it with harpsichord, and playing alien, unadorned Ellington standards.

title: Ballad of a Tryhard
description: Accompanied by strings, sax, and piano, the Toronto musician sorts through his past on an intimate collection of orchestral pop, bursting with hooks.

title: Continuance
description: On their third collaborative project, the duo makes minor but strong tweaks to a reliable system.

title: Regards to the End
description: The complex, referential new album from the New York-based composer responds to historical crises with sprawling orchestral pop.

title: Donda 2
description: Released exclusively on a device called the Stem Player, the first version of Kanye’s 11th album is lackluster and undercooked. It does not bode well for any future updates or revamps.

title: The Tipping Point
description: The legendary pop duo’s first new album in 18 years approaches the challenges of middle life with familiar sensitivity and shared intimacy. It’s a strikingly unguarded and forthright record.

title: Forget Your Own Face
description: The Toronto noise-pop duo specialize in harsh music and heavy topics. Their latest record can be lighthearted, but the resentment at its heart feels more outwardly pointed than ever.

title: Jupiter’s Purse
description: The Dallas-based producer and musician sings an ode to the dissected self on their fully-formed debut EP, a metallic amalgam of trip-hop and electronic soul.

title: Wild Loneliness
description: The indie band’s 12th album uses a moodier, more subdued palette to get to the heart of some fun topics like fear and ambivalence in the face of environmental and societal ruin.

title: Becoming Undone
description: Inspired by the grimness of the present moment and grief over a loved one’s death, the Detroit electro duo is at the height of its dark powers.

title: caroline
description: Five years in the making, the UK band’s debut accomplishes something nearly impossible for a largely instrumental post-rock album: to project urgency and timelessness simultaneously.

title: I’m Not Sorry, I Was Just Being Me
description: On its debut album, the UK duo spins deadpan tales about the mundanities of existence over a desolate, desert backdrop recalling PJ Harvey and Nick Cave.

title: I Need A Job​.​.​.​So I Can Buy More Auto​-​Tune
description: On the third album since his Justin Vernon-assisted 2018 comeback, the mischievous singer heaps on the Auto-Tune, but his songwriting has more in common with his Southern-fried soul of the 1970s.

title: A Time to Love
description: After a long wait and an intense build-up, Stevie Wonder’s 2005 collab-heavy return is unerringly stately, sometimes bracing, proof that the artist had endured.

title: Hotter Than July
description: Stevie Wonder capped off his classic era with the ecstatic 1980 album Hotter Than July, a tour of summer sounds that encompasses all the meanings of heat.

title: Innervisions
description: The astonishing Innervisions is suffused in the sound and politics of 1973, a conceptually ambitious and sonically innovative pillar of Stevie Wonder’s classic years.

title: Talking Book
description: Stevie Wonder’s second legendary album of 1972 contains heartbreaking hits about love and social crisis. Its revolutionary use of the synthesizer humanized the instrument to a degree never heard before.

title: Up-Tight
description: Stevie Wonder’s early Motown career hit its peak on 1966’s Up-Tight, cementing his role as someone born to make music not only as a career but as a calling.

title: Angel in Realtime
description: Led by the charismatic Dave Le’aupepe, the stadium rock quintet’s wildly ambitious third album is intimate in its details but rarely anything other than IMAX-sized in its proportions.

title: God Don’t Make Mistakes
description: On his most personal project to date, the Buffalo rapper laces intimate narratives with battle-ready barbs over an ornate collage of haunting boom-bap.

title: 4 Hands
description: After decades of making music together, the two friends sit down to an unusual collaboration: a series of duets recorded on a single piano, in alternating takes.

title: Plonk
description: On his first album as Huerco S. in six years, the Kansas musician trades his customary ambient textures for an hour’s worth of intricate, off-center head trips.

title: Blurry
description: On his debut album, the Berlin musician sets aside his techno proclivities in favor of a moody journey into a more innocent era of electronic music.

title: Digital Roses Don’t Die
description: Though the rapper takes questionable creative risks on his fifth album, he’s still capable of bringing scenes to life with a wide eye and a sharp pen.

title: Boundary Object
description: Recorded in real time and released without further edits, the Hungarian musician’s dizzyingly unstable experiments in rhythm and timbre revel in the plasticity of sound.

title: Limbs
description: The English musician and actor’s second album places her spectacular vibrato front and center, shadowed by subtle but effective orchestration. Listening feels like a bracing walk through winter moorland.

title: Chain of Command
description: The Soundcloud rapper’s latest album offers a natural point of entry to his gripping aesthetic, distilling his virtuosity in a series of distinct, yet successful cuts.

title: Prey//IV
description: The full-length solo debut from the former Crystal Castles singer is a dark, extreme pop record about abuse, power, and regaining control.

title: The Long Count
description: The chilling and provocative new album from the electroacoustic producer is a work of speculative sonic fiction, reimagining the sounds of ancient Mayan musical history.

title: Cowboy Tears
description: Back from retirement again, the polarizing, meme-powered pop singer takes up “cowboy emo”: breakup songs with a cartoonish twang and schlocky Western aesthetics.

title: Everything Was Forever
description: More than two decades into its career, the band formerly known as British Sea Power sounds newly energized, eagerly plotting new routes to familiar emotional peaks.

title: Starfruit
description: The trio’s fifth album further smooths out their neo-soul sound while celebrating the voices that inspired them along the way.

title: Sad Cities
description: The semi-anonymous singer has changed her mind about retirement, but almost nothing else. Her first album since 2013 sets emotional miniatures to widescreen Italo disco and dinner-for-one city pop.

title: 2 Alivë
description: The 21-year-old Portland rapper isn’t doing anything all that new, but he has a refreshing album-focused approach, best listened to as one continuous stream, getting lost in the noisy madness.

title: CM10: Free Game
description: The Memphis rapper takes a well-earned victory lap on the latest edition of his Cocaine Muzik series, a consistent double album filled with reliable raps and familiar beats.

title: Suburban Lawns
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 1981 debut from the mysterious Los Angeles post-punk band, who developed a cult following and vanished just as quickly.

title: Blackberry Rose
description: Nearly 50 years after he recorded perhaps the first country album by an openly gay person, Seattle folk singer Patrick Haggerty returns with a follow-up. In all of his songs, he’s equal parts empath and scold, a soft touch with a sharp tongue.

title: Bobby Weir & Wolf Bros: Live in Colorado
description: Where Dead & Company emphasize the Grateful Dead’s psychedelic spectacle, Bob Weir’s rootsy trio offers a more intimate reimagining of his former group’s historic countercultural songbook.

title: Ngbaka EP
description: Known for elaborate handmade instruments and stage costumes, the veteran Congolese eco-punks commit their frenetic, highly collaborative sound to record for the first time.

title: Life on Earth
description: Alynda Segarra’s powerful eighth album exudes a glorious irreverence. Their self-described “nature punk” songs are both intimate and immense, and they’ve never sounded more honest or self-possessed.

title: B Flat A
description: The Polish band’s latest shows that they don’t make protest music so much as process music, indulging the ugliest aspects of post-punk and post-hardcore as a means to protect what’s good and beautiful in this world.

title: Once Twice Melody
description: With panoramic proportions and gleaming finishes, the band’s sprawling eighth album luxuriates in the rhapsody of sensation itself. You don’t listen to Once Twice Melody, you dissolve into it.

title: Pike vs the Automaton
description: On his first solo album, the Sleep and High on Fire frontman hits the garage for a comfortable blend of his signature heavy metal sounds.

title: Soundtrack [313]
description: Gleaming with ambient intent, melodic classicism, and clean lines, this 1996 classic bridges the gap between Detroit techno and Tangerine Dream.

title: Harold and Maude (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
description: To celebrate the cult classic’s 50th anniversary, a new collection of Cat Stevens’ music for the film—including songs later covered by Elliott Smith and others—finally becomes widely available.

title: Krüller
description: The San Diego artist incorporates a grungy alt-rock influence into his grinding industrial music, revealing a tuneful, human side to his work.

title: Just for You
description: On his latest album, the Massachusetts rapper recognizes the value of sticking to a formula and gently retooling what works instead of drawing attention to what doesn’t.

title: Heaux Tales, Mo’ Tales: The Deluxe
description: On a triumphant deluxe edition of her 2021 opus, the Philadelphia singer lays the groundwork for growth with several new songs and interludes, including an appearance from Issa Rae.

title: Good Morning Gorgeous
description: The sheer strength and breadth of Mary J. Blige’s voice is like comfort food. Her 14th studio album mixes soaring, soulful affirmations with some confusing collaborations.

title: BADモード
description: Decades into their career, this J-pop superstar continues to evolve—both musically and personally. BADモード reads like a friend’s gentle reminder that we’re always coming into our own.

title: Asha’s Awakening
description: Incorporating South Asian instruments and singing in English and Hindi, the New York singer-songwriter crafts a concept album from the perspective of a Punjabi space princess.

title: Heterosexuality
description: Backed by industrial noise, drum machines, and synths, the Philadelphia-based songwriter rages at systems of oppression on a bleak, troubling record of nearly unrelenting hostility.

title: Glitch Princess
description: The pioneering second album from the avant-pop artist is a darkly nuanced look at identity, technology, and death, where personal disasters occur at the same scale as the actual apocalypse.

title: Give Me the Future
description: The pop-rock superstars attempt a concept album about virtual reality that is almost perverse in its inability or unwillingness to develop its premise beyond the most basic and obvious elements.

title: Drive My Car - Original Soundtrack
description: The Japanese experimental musician’s score for the lauded new film by Ryusuke Hamaguchi possesses a cool remove, mirroring the film’s glacial profundity with organic nuance and contemplative improvisation.

title: Visitor
description: The second album from the Philadelphia noise-pop band comes with some great new sounds, but dials down some of the thrill and fervor that made their debut so exceptional.

title: Lighten Up
description: Taking influence from the legends of Laurel Canyon, the Nashville songwriter crafts an earnest, tranquil listen that opens up a rich world of detail.

title: Symbolic
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 1995 album by the incalculably influential Florida death metal band, the most melodic and refined album of their career.

title: Lucifer on the Sofa
description: Two decades into their career, Spoon return with loud, low-down, melodious rock record almost without sacrificing any of their savory nuance and inscrutability.

title: Disrespectful
description: Brash, rude, and definitely not sober, the Yorkshire bassline trio return with a new mixtape full of soulful house samples and performance-art level idiocy.

title: W
description: On the minimalist companion to 2020’s NO, the Japanese trio lands a delicate balance of dream pop and drone. It feels like a sanctuary.

title: Never Stop Texting Me
description: The Texas experimentalists set aside their drone and ASMR proclivities in favor of Auto-Tuned riffs on hyperpop, indulging in plenty of deadpan jokes and self-deprecating swagger along the way.

title: Earthling
description: The Pearl Jam leader’s first solo album in over a decade is an amiable, tuneful set with appearances from Stevie Wonder, Ringo Starr, and Elton John.

title: Dragon New Warm Mountain I Believe in You
description: Big Thief’s ambitious yet unburdened fifth album is a 20-song epic of kaleidoscopic invention, striking beauty, and wigged-out humor, rambling far beyond the bounds of their previous work.

title: IRÉ
description: The New York-based Colombian rock band updates its powerful live chops with careful studio experimentation, balancing  psychedelic sounds with a sense of sociopolitical urgency.

title: Where You Are
description: The South African 23-year-old follows up his scene-sketching debut with this taut eight-track collection of luxurious amapiano designed for the genre’s growing mainstream audience.

title: The Highest in the Land
description: The final album from the mercurial post-punk project offers a wellspring of quotable surrealism, showing the substance and self-definition of the late Pat Fish.

title: Catch Me If You Can
description: The Nigerian singer has the writing and vocal chops to best most of the leading men of Afropop. But his self-proclaimed transformation feels like a talented artist simply conforming to trends.

title: Shortwave Memories
description: Geir Jenssen’s return to ambient techno captures him at his frostiest. It’s his largest-scale and most meticulously crafted release in some time.

title: Electroacoustic Works
description: The composer’s electronic music dates back to the 1950s yet still sounds radical today. This five-disc box set illustrates the spirit of possibility animating even his most forbidding pieces.

title: DFTK
description: The debut album from the Young Thug protégé is an exhilarating opening salvo by an artist who only occasionally seems in full control of his considerable talent—which is half the fun.

title: Ants From Up There
description: The exceptional second album from the London group plays like a slow burn to a triumphant finale. Softer and more melodic, the band remains just as challenging and delightfully confounding as ever.

title: Candid
description: The Philly rapper examines growth and longing with a mature assuredness, imbuing her latest album with moments of modest warmth.

title: JP5000
description: With killer beat selections and a fresh sense of focus, the New York rapper’s latest project exudes the unnerving calm and clarity that come with years of refinement.

title: C91
description: Modeled after the NME’s scene-making C86 compilation, this 59-track collection captures the sound of British alternative rock in 1991, in all its glorious chaos.

title: Pompeii
description: Cate Le Bon’s wondrous sixth album exists in a waking dreamscape whose locked-in grooves approach the unknowable at slanted angles.

title: Let The Festivities Begin!
description: Produced by Franz Ferdinand’s Alex Kapranos, the multi-national group fuses Argentine cumbia, Peruvian chicha, and Turkish psych into a giddy sound that leans unabashedly retro.

title: Daughter
description: Collaging field recordings and instrumental scraps, Grouper and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma construct an elegatic tribute to the life and work of their late friend, filmmaker Paul Clipson.

title: Few Good Things
description: On his latest carefree and careworn album, the Chicago rapper turns softer and more melodic, exploring his provisional success and the unanswered questions it keeps raising.

title: Junkyard
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Nick Cave’s early punk band and their pulpy, lurid, and legendary 1982 album.

title: Round Trip: Ornette Coleman on Blue Note
description: What happens after you set the world on fire? On six Blue Note LPs following landmark albums The Shape of Jazz to Come and Free Jazz, the mercurial saxophonist endeavored to find out.

title: Dope Don’t Sell Itself
description: The Atlanta rapper still has an ear and charisma on his latest album, but the songs are more like templates than novel creations. For the first time, he sounds predictable.

title: Time Skiffs
description: After a prolific period of experimentation, Animal Collective return with an album that achieves a peaceful equilibrium between their immersive 3D soundscaping and innate melodic charms.

title: Dissolution Wave
description: The Indiana shoegaze trio returns with a songs-first, vibes-second concept album that’s both punchy and immersive.

title: Planet EP
description: Featuring demos, outtakes, and a quietly powerful Björk cover, this EP from the Massachusetts songwriter feels like a gentle exhale.

title: Old Gold
description: World-building takes precedence over the music on this Melbourne producer’s concept album, a nuanced retelling of the 1850s Victoria gold rush made up of MIDI banjos and artificial sounds.

title: For McCoy
description: The Japanese multi-instrumentalist enlists Jim O’Rourke for an unusual fusion of jazz improv, musique concrète, and plaintive pop that pays tribute to Law & Order’s Jack McCoy.
The band’s open-armed fifth album looks to make amends, situating our human responsibilities within a natural world no less powerful and vulnerable than we are.

title: Nakama
description: Collaborators including Circuit des Yeux’s Haley Fohr and members of Mdou Moctar’s band reinterpret the guitar virtuoso’s songs, reinforcing his growing stature as a singer-songwriter.

title: Little Green House
description: The Connecticut quintet’s debut is the work of pop-punk professionals, modeled after the genre’s mainstream breakthroughs in the early 2000s.

title: Laurel Hell
description: Mitski’s sixth album is an austere, nuanced, and disaffected indie-pop record that, in part, addresses her turbulent relationship with her own career.

title: Motordrome
description: The Danish singer-songwriter’s powerhouse voice can wring genuine catharsis out of even the gaudiest pop, but on her third album, the muted, anonymous production too often holds her back.

title: Colors
description: The prolific rapper continues to push himself to vocal extremes, but his new album seldom coalesces his virtuosity into something that surpasses his signature work.

title: FACE
description: The Detroit rapper’s world is bleak and flashy in equal measure. On the followup to 2021’s Unfuckwitable, he’s getting better at balancing his opposing tendencies.

title: The Umbrella Again
description: Steered by his nasally voice and laid-back delivery, one of the original members of Team Eastside delivers a no-frills, 25-track Detroit rap album.

title: Summer of Soul (...Or, When The Revolution Could Not Be Televised) Original Motion Picture Soundtrack
description: The soundtrack to Questlove’s excellent documentary on the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival tells a nuanced story of Black creativity and perseverance at the end of a transformative decade.

title: Last Room
description: The Connecticut DIY duo struggles to shed their influences on this newly remastered and reissued record, yet they still manage to bring a unique virtuosity and vitality to downcast guitar pop.

title: Fantasy
description: The Montreal producer sounds liberated on his latest EP, an idealized evocation of the club made up of fleeting breakbeats and ribbony synths.

title: forever music
description: On her fifth album, the Australian singer-songwriter steps away from the bleak feelings of her early, glitch-scoured work, reflecting this newfound clarity with unadorned arrangements for voice and keys.

title: Island of Noise
description: Jack Cooper’s vision as a songwriter and bandleader comes into focus on the most cohesive album of his career: a fantasyland hybrid of elegant folk rock and understated free jazz.

title: The Listening
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 2003 debut by the North Carolina rap trio, a ridiculously hard throwback album that plugged hip-hop’s golden era into the internet age.

title: Let England Shake - Demos
description: The UK musician offers a revealing look at the making of her acclaimed 2011 album Let England Shake—just the latest in a growing series of behind-the-scenes demo collections.

title: Three Dimensions Deep
description: The pop-R&B singer’s long-awaited debut follows a line from crippling self-doubt to pure confidence, adopting a glossy and funky vibe fortified by her exceptional voice and songwriting.

title: Anaïs Mitchell
description: On her first album of all-new solo material since 2012, the Vermont-based folk singer reflects on her life with measured reverence.

title: Camo
description: The Brooklyn producer’s heavily abstracted ambient music offers a choice between deep listening or blissful distraction. It’s equally gratifying either way.

title: Shoals
description: Instead of a reinvention, the London band’s latest album jumps at the chance to blend in with every other rock act on the festival circuit.

title: on to better things
description: The 22-year-old singer fits into a burgeoning pop niche where angsty emo rap, frothy trap-pop, sunny Top 40 choruses, and punchy pop-punk riffs congeal.

title: Havasu
description: David Bazan reflects on small-town adolescence with an insular and empathetic album about tedium, disappointment, and simmering tension.

title: Brightside
description: On an exhilarating but exhausting new EP, the Indonesian rapper strives for maturity but remains at his best when he’s at his silliest.

title: Love of Plastic
description: Neither arch nor brittle, this is the Japanese electronic musician’s most approachable and generous collection to date: “plastic” as in “malleable,” not “artificial.”

title: Gangsta Grillz: We Set the Trends
description: The Dipset capo wins not by breaking new ground but by alternating between trying existing trends and throwing back to the sounds of his past.

title: Sin Miedo EP
description: Brooklyn-based musician Kam Tambini layers roaring guitars, Latin rhythms, and his own low-pitched, sighing vocals to explore the mundanity of city life.

title: Tongues
description: Vivifying scenes from her debut novel, the Inuk experimentalist and throat-singer marries fiery condemnations of oppression with tender words of protection for future generations.

title: Long Live Young Dolph
description: On this compilation, artists in Young Dolph’s circle keep the rapper’s legacy of love and loyalty alive, giving the project a clear sense of purpose.

title: The Runner (Original Soundtrack)
description: On the soundtrack to an imagistic new film project, the darkwave duo’s limited palette verges on claustrophobia. Their winning formula hasn’t changed, but the music lacks drive.

title: Strictly a One-Eyed Jack
description: Featuring several collaborations with Bruce Springsteen, the self-produced new album from the 70-year-old songwriter is overwhelmingly bleak—but its best moments prove he can still surprise us.

title: Distance on Ground
description: The collaborative audio-visual project layers Maxwell Sterling’s double bass and Martha Skye Murphy’s limber soprano with a variety of subtle tones and textures that lure the mind to journey where the body cannot.

title: Asakusa Light
description: His career revived by the 2015 anthology Sounds from the Far East, the Japanese electronic musician and video-game composer returns to the radiant deep house that won him fans like the late Larry Levan.

title: Age of Apathy
description: The Irish American singer-songwriter taps into the propulsion of prime Joni Mitchell: a restless mind bouncing against the blur of one’s surroundings.

title: Club Sentimientos, Vol. 2 EP
description: Across three blissfully spaced-out tracks, the New York producer continues to explore the fusion of left-field dance music and reggaetón.

title: Epics in Minutes / Demo 7"
description: Reissues of early recordings reveal a blistering, primordial version of Fucked Up, steeped in the tight-knit Toronto punk scene they called home.

title: Third Eye Blind
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit a shining jewel of ’90s pop-rock, an album full of melodies, amphetamines, and hubris.

title: Tissues
description: An hour-long excerpt of an experimental performance at the Tate Modern in 2019, Tissues is rooted in opera but extends the sounds, themes, and harrowing moods of the Berlin-based musician’s electronic work.

title: From a Bird’s Eye View
description: Cordae’s latest album proves he doesn’t have an ethos or a sense of excitement that separates his music from other rappers with a working-class view.

title: Optimism
description: With the boiled-down quality of a good short story collection, the debut album from the Texas songwriter is cryptic, bewildering, and daringly simple.

title: The Overload
description: The Leeds band’s mouthy and acerbic take on Brexit-era post-punk has the humor, polish, and storytelling of classic Britpop.

title: Dodging Dues
description: The New Jersey sextet’s fifth studio album is an easeful tour of muscular riff-rock, noodly song suites, and curtsying pastoral folk.

title: Acrobatic Thoughts
description: On his vivid and eccentric new album, the Roman-born electronic producer smooths down some of his edges and sinks deeper into an air of wide-eyed rapture.

artist: Wadada Leo Smith / Henry Kaiser / Alex Varty
title: Pacifica Koral Reef
description: Improvising on trumpet and two guitars, the avant-garde composer and his collaborators mourn the natural world while asking us to forget what we know about conventional musical hierarchies.

title: The Boy Named If
description: On his 32nd studio album, Elvis Costello treats the traditional rock quartet as the ideal medium for delicacy, concision, wit, and the occasional harangue.

title: Storm Queen
description: On her self-produced second album, the Melbourne folk singer embellishes her stark, bluesy songwriting with symphonic touches that occasionally get in the way of her daring vocal performances.

artist: Riad Awwad / Hanan Awwad / Mahmoud Darwish
title: The Intifada 1987
description: Recorded in Jerusalem in 1987, Riad Awwad’s protest album is part ode to the beauty of homeland, part historical document of Palestinian struggle, and part instruction manual for revolution.

title: Fragments
description: As he evolves to match modern conceptions of chillout music, downtempo producer Simon Green lands on a sound that’s pleasant, current, and unoriginal.

title: Old Dead Young: B-Sides & Rarities
description: The Canadian indie rock band sorts through a largely subdued grab bag of material on this career-spanning set, highlighted by offbeat experiments and homespun, intimate moments.

title: XVI
description: On its Thurston Moore-boosted debut, the Miami quartet offers an enchanting swirl of indie rock, dream pop, and acid-funk odysseys whose relaxed mood belies a restless philosophical spirit.

title: CAPRISONGS
description: The singer’s new mixtape is a playful and adventurous flex, full of errant, shapeshifting compositions that flirt with choral music and Afrobeats, schoolyard chants and squeak-rapping.

title: Nick of Time
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Bonnie Raitt’s 1989 blockbuster comeback, a genre-fluid album about love, disappointment, and aging.

title: Live at Montreux Jazz Festival
description: This ensemble performance from 2018 offers an ideal introduction to the Swedish songwriter’s work, showcasing her vocal virtuosity and gothic drama.

title: Covers
description: Featuring songs by Frank Ocean, Lana Del Rey, Nick Cave, and more, Chan Marshall’s third collection of covers is her widest ranging yet, illustrating her talent for radical reinvention.

title: Sick!
description: Earl Sweatshirt used to make you sift through the mud to find the gold. On his latest album, the nuggets are gleaming right on the surface.

title: DS4Ever
description: The Atlanta rapper’s latest album is monotonous, short on the quirks and out-of-body experiences of his better projects.

title: Wandering
description: Taking influence from drone, metal, and noise, the latest project from the mercurial electronic producer is a brooding collaborative album that relishes in its own bleakness.

title: Retrospective (2016-2021)
description: This 20-track collection of music by the prolific Spanish ambient producer feels like submerging into a warm bath for 95 minutes.

title: A World of Service
description: On her debut for Berlin’s Ostgut Ton label, the Spanish-born producer trades industrial techno for more unpredictable hybrids drawn from hyperpop, trip-hop, and IDM.

title: Magic
description: Nas is a pointillist, better at writing couplets than albums, and Magic proves he’s still a transcendent rapper when he allows himself to be.

title: Dartland
description: The Seattle-based emo band longs for the unattainable with a sense of modesty and restraint that can be as frustrating as it is endearing.

title: Antidawn
description: Burial’s longest release in years doubles down on his signature sounds and downcast mood. A collaged chorus of voices holds together a windswept expanse of undulating nothingness.

title: sometimes i feel like i have no friends
description: Using her customary palette of field recordings, captured conversations, and instrumental contributions from friends, the Texas composer lays bare her darkest thoughts about friendship and solitude.

title: Came
description: On his shape-shifting second album, the 18-year-old Vietnamese artist wrings beauty out of chaos with fractured, vignette-like compositions.

title: WAKE UP LUCKI
description: Over synth-heavy beats by the co-founder of Philadelphia's Working on Dying collective, the Chicago rapper writes intensely diaristic songs delivered with numb detachment.

title: Dawn FM
description: Conceptualized around listening to a retro-pop radio station in purgatory, Abel Tesfaye’s fifth album is the most thoughtful, melodic, and revealing project of his career.

title: FabricLive.37
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit an infamous 2007 DJ mix that helped transform dubstep from a bubbling scene to a global phenomenon.

title: Carnegie Hall 1970
description: A captivating solo performance at Manhattan’s most haunted showroom, the latest release in Neil Young’s ongoing archival project showcases a fascinating pivot point in the young songwriter’s career.

title: Nonante-Cinq
description: The Belgian singer’s second album explores her gift for imbuing joyful, self-possessed dance pop with bittersweet emotion.

title: Archives Volume 2: The Reprise Years (1968-1971)
description: Spanning the years between her debut and Blue, this 122-song set documents the hard work of exploration, revision, and rejection that shaped the songwriter’s first masterpiece. It is a humanizing wonder.

title: 4Nem
description: Almost three years since his last solo project, the 26-year-old rapper continues to reimagine and reinterpret his influences, which is part of what makes his new music feel so alive.

title: Stars
description: With richly textured psychedelic folk music, the Los Angeles artist draws complex emotions out of simple love songs.

title: Wildest Dreams
description: Once again fusing R&B and retro synth pop, the Toronto duo’s third album revels in the impermanence of intimacy. The production and singing dazzle, even when the emotions feel hollow.

title: Live Life Fast
description: The Compton rapper’s second album occasionally showcases the magic he can make, but the music is largely static, a rollercoaster operating on a straight track.

title: Scenic Drive
description: With a stacked guest list, the 23-year-old singer’s latest mixtape showcases his curatorial instincts even as it cruises through a familiar landscape of soft, shapeless R&B.

title: Grizzly Peak
description: On its warm and reflective new album, the Bay Area duo offers the most plainly pretty songs of its career. The stakes are high but the mood is anything but tense.

title: MOVES: 5 Years of Culture - Afrobeats / Rap & Drill
description: Five years after a landmark compilation that helped introduce the then-emergent sound of UK Afrobeats, London’s Moves Recordings takes stock of a half-decade of innovations in Black British music.

title: Fiat Lux
description: Drawing on Mediterranean folk, Georgian laments, and the 12th century mystic Hildegard von Bingen, the Catalan duo’s debut album is musically unique yet emotionally familiar.

title: Mother of Pearl
description: The Los Angeles–based musicians explore the spaces between their respective styles, yielding an ethereal, richly textured fusion of neo-classical and musique concréte.

title: Blind Date Party
description: Featuring collaborators from across the Drag City universe and a repertoire of gospel, country, pop, and rock covers, Bill Callahan and Bonnie “Prince” Billy’s lockdown double-album is playful and spirited.

title: Barn
description: Neil Young’s decision to prioritize immediacy over craft in his later years means these tunes arrive lovingly weathered, but rarely go anywhere in particular.

title: The Nearer the Fountain, More Pure the Stream Flows
description: Initially conceived as an orchestral tribute to Iceland’s remote majesty, the Blur and Gorillaz frontman’s second solo album blossoms into a wide-angle commentary on grief, loss, and climate crisis.

title: Breathe Suite EP
description: The London jazz musician’s sprawling suite explores the vital function of breath in times of distress. The music can be tranquil, but it also formally mimics the act of calming down.

title: Peace and Offerings EP
description: The UK dance star downshifts on her first new collection in five years, embracing smoky, understated R&B with moody arrangements and a flirty touch.

title: Fighting Demons
description: Juice WRLD’s second posthumous album attempts to be more of the same, highlighting the best and worst qualities of a generational talent gone too soon.

title: Resident Alien
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Spacehog’s 1995 debut, an architecturally sound, occasionally great, always amusing collection of transatlantic power pop.

title: Live in Brighton 1975
description: The second album in Mute’s planned series of archival Can shows captures a group figuring things out in real time. After 30 tentative minutes, things turn transcendent.

title: Richer Than I Ever Been
description: The Miami rapper is still bringing you into his world of opulence and hustlers’ theme music, but the view is more refined.

title: From the Bayou
description: Birdman’s presence is largely intrusive on the pair’s joint project. It’s YoungBoy’s versatility that keeps the album afloat.

title: Live From Blackalachia
description: Recorded in the Blue Ridge Mountains with a seven-piece band, Moses Sumney’s first live album and film find freedom and beauty in the isolation of the forest.

title: Cahoots (50th Anniversary Edition)
description: Unraveling from the pressure of success and celebrity, the Band moved to a new studio in Woodstock and made their fourth album, a stiff and scattershot record that is somewhat enlivened by a new reissue.

title: Observatory
description: The Wrens’ songwriter Kevin Whelan’s bittersweet solo debut is a rousing, unabashedly sentimental indie rock album that stakes out a sweet spot between the anthemic and the intimate.

title: Broken Hearts & Dirty Windows: Songs of John Prine, Vol. 2
description: A second installment of John Prine covers includes some of the legendary songwriter’s best-known material, illustrating how his legacy—and the definition of Americana—has shifted since 2010.

title: Forfolks
description: On his new solo album, the Tortoise guitarist blends loops and improvisations in dazzling ways. It sounds like jazz but moves like a soft techno dream.

title: Neuromantic
description: Reissued on vinyl for the first time in four decades, the Yellow Magic Orchestra drummer and vocalist’s 1981 solo album isolates his infectious hooks, powerful rhythms, and modern pop sensibility.

title: Juju Music
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Nigerian superstar King Sunny Adé’s 1982 international breakthrough, an album whose complex fusion of musical traditions produced a singularly captivating groove.

title: Brilliant Adventure (1992-2001)
description: This box set of Bowie’s work in the 1990s—a period when he reasserted his role as the godfather of alternative music—houses the lost album Toy and makes a case for a bold, divisive era of experiments.

title: Big Sleepover
description: Shrewd beat choices (and Killer Mike) liven up a lopsided collaboration between two longtime Dungeon Family members who still share undeniable chemistry.

title: Embryo EP
description: This grimy new EP from the Gary, Indiana producer has the unfinished edge of a sketch, pointing toward the dancefloor while showcasing her twin forces of invincibility and vulnerability.

title: The Time of Foxgloves
description: As he approaches his eightieth year, the veteran folk craftsman embraces good times and creature comforts on a collection of homespun tunes that radiates his familiar charm and insight.

title: Romeo
description: On his second album, the London producer summons the divine with intoxicating, emotional dance music fit for a crowded warehouse.

title: Cong!
description: Nic Oogjes’ lounge-lizard alter ego makes heady, gleefully ridiculous no wave pastiche held together by flamboyance and a predilection for showmanship.

title: Balens Cho (Hot Candles)
description: The New Jersey rapper makes Haiti the main character of his latest project, balancing social context with a sense of intimacy and urgency.

title: Concrete
description: Using sparse language and baroque instrumentation, the London artist explores captivity and control over this spectral three song EP.

title: Wave Your Moonlight Hat for the Snowfall Train
description: The ambient dream-pop duo’s fourth album is split between fragile vocal meditations and instrumentals as delicate as origami cranes.

title: Der Lange Marsch
description: Wolfgang Voigt treats the seventh album from his beloved ambient techno moniker like a retrospective, filtering familiar tropes into a comforting pulse. But a disturbing hint of tinnitus lurks in the margins.

title: Old Friends New Friends
description: Collecting 12 years of solo piano recordings, the Berlin composer explores some of his quietest, most intimate material yet, in which the creaking of the pedal is often as audible as the notes.

title: All These Years
description: On these solo piano performances, the musician known for his work with Justin Vernon, Hiss Golden Messenger, and more suggests that peaceful solitude can offer its own high.

title: fabric presents SHERELLE
description: Cruising at her habitual 160 beats per minute, the rising London DJ mixes old-school jungle techno, acid rave, breakbeat hardcore, and footwork into an exhilarating 75-minute set.

title: KICK ii / KicK iii / kick iiii / kiCK iiiii
description: Arca’s ambitious musical cycle concludes with four albums spanning reggaeton, club experiments, and tender synth lullabies. It’s a slippery, unwieldy, mind-bending collection of sound design that drives home the ur-theme of all her music: transformation.

title: Woke Up Right Handed EP
description: Delivering his most interesting work in years, the UK techno producer throws convention to the winds while indulging a dark sense of humor that feeds off the preposterous and the grotesque.

title: Peace Meter
description: On her debut solo album under her own name, the Screaming Females frontperson reintroduces herself, placing the focus on her remarkable singing voice.

title: Rap?
description: The Philadelphia rapper’s new EP may be more straightforward than usual, but even at her most conventional, Whack is at least attempting to keep you off-balance.

title: Tide Turns Eternal
description: On their lush, formidable debut, the “dream-doom” duo of Tomb Mold’s Derrick Vella and Innumerable Forms’ Justin DeTore illustrate how emotionally boundless metal can be.

title: It’s All Smiles
description: On his full-length debut, the 24-year-old singer’s chameleonic tenor pierces through the Dirty Hit template and finds a natural fit in pouty pop-rock and gauzy trip-hop.

title: Foreign Exchange
description: The duo offers a tight, cohesive project that binds Gud’s experienced pop precision with Papi’s uncontrolled intensity.

title: The Romance of Affliction
description: Borrowing the clean hooks of metalcore and scene-chewing flourishes of MySpace emo, the San Diego band’s second album takes an unflinchingly honest look at impending doom.

title: I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the folk-rock duo's darkly holistic 1974 debut, a quixotic blend of the old and the new.

title: Julius Eastman, Vol. 1: Femenine
description: For the first installment of its proposed seven-album anthology of the late composer’s work, the California collective breathes new life into his ecstatic minimalist masterpiece.

title: Ascension Codes
description: Following the deaths of two core members, the pioneering Florida metal band searches for celestial answer to earthly woes. It’s as close to a return-to-form as they’ve ever made.

title: The Sacrifice EP
description: Armed with field recordings and ancient folklore, the peripatetic electronic musician pauses to construct a resonant, mysterious portrait of the rugged Welsh landscape.

title: Spencer (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack)
description: The alternately beautiful and unnerving score to Pablo Larraín’s surreal film about Princess Diana captures the elegance of a royal holiday and the horror of feeling trapped inside of it.

title: Ocean to Ocean
description: On her 16th album, begun early this year as the UK entered its third lockdown, the Cornwall-based singer-songwriter grapples with personal loss, the cruelty of the world, and the will to keep going.

title: Queen of My World
description: The second album from guitarist Betsy Wright and drummer Laura King revels in a good time, backing up their bite with instrumental brawn.

title: Switched on Ra
description: After covering Sun Ra on 2017’s Bajas Fresh, the Chicago trio fires up a passel of arcane vintage synths and interprets eight more songs by the cosmic jazz legend.

title: Are You Happy EP
description: Collaborating with producer Lynyn, the chameleonic Chicago musician offers a toned-down vision of his exuberant experimental pop.

title: Open Arms to Open Us
description: The Chicago multi-instrumentalist and composer’s second album crisscrosses genres and eras, sprawling in its ambition and surprisingly precise in its attack.

title: Water
description: After the comparatively bleak experimental club sounds of 2018’s Power, the Berlin-based Texan producer embraces the warmth and intimacy of slow-paced R&B, sounding newly at ease.

title: Giant + Guitar
description: A new reissue of the Egyptian guitarist’s 1974 breakthrough showcases his virtuosic playing and groundbreaking blend of styles.

title: Tell Me What You Miss the Most
description: On her hushed second album, the Chicago artist writes minimal, unpredictable songs that explore the in-between states of relationships with subtlety and grace.

title: At My Piano
description: Featuring instrumental renditions of many of the Beach Boys’ greatest hits, this collection of solo piano performances feels disappointingly bare and anonymous.

title: The Clearing
description: The New York experimental musician takes his own stutter as the starting point for an album that is both a theoretical investigation of speech dysfluency and a piece of resistance art.

title: I Thought of You
description: On the first new album under her own name since 2012, the Canadian songwriter makes her voice the focus. Her songs feel instantly familiar, like smaller pieces of a timeless story.

title: The Light-Emitting Diamond Cutter Scriptures
description: Ferreira’s latest album is rich and rewarding, the mark of a prolific artist arriving at the perfect unity between content and presentation.

title: Body/Dilloway/Head
description: Kim Gordon and Bill Nace’s guitar duo collides with noise icon Aaron Dilloway’s inscrutable electronic methods, resulting in a thrilling mutation of all three artists’ signature sounds.

title: DJ-Kicks
description: Balancing contemporary house and techno with detours into footwork, gqom, and more, the Canadian musician’s mix reveals the range of influences behind her own singular brand of synth pop.

title: Voyage to Mars
description: Josianne Boivin’s full-length debut gestures toward space opera, but her lonely disco and lo-fi aesthetic are better suited for sleepy introspection about your place on Earth.

title: Buds
description: For all its slacker-rock credentials, the Connecticut band could rarely be described as loose. Its third album is a short, hooky celebration of friendship and fuzz pedals.

title: Diana
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit a landmark disco and pop album, a dazzling and fabulous collaboration between Chic and Diana Ross.

title: The Power of the Dog (Music From the Netflix Film)
description: Like his scores for Paul Thomas Anderson, the Radiohead guitarist’s soundtrack to Jane Campion’s new film invokes the 20th-century avant-garde, full of noble brooding and tormented ecstasy.

title: Henki
description: The eccentric English songwriter and the prolific Finnish rock group collaborate for an album that routes ancient plant life into deeply human stories of toil, tragedy, and the afterlife.

title: Blacklight
description: A solid serving of meat-and-potatoes rap, the duo’s first joint project thrives on a sense of comfort and familiarity more often than not.

title: Deciphering the Message
description: On his latest project, the jazz drummer and innovative producer brings the heart of the famous Blue Note catalog into the present.

title: Soaked in Indigo Moonlight
description: Long known for his dusty, slow-motion take on UK bass, the London producer makes a surprising turn toward pop on his debut album, without stifling any of his experimental instincts.

title: Reporting Live (From the Back of the Roads)
description: The British-Congolese rapper’s ambitious new mixtape proves there’s fertile ground to be found in the interplay between grime, UK drill, and velvety Afropop.

title: Frailty
description: The official debut from the young digicore producer and songwriter is riveting, a shapeshifting emo-electronic record that sounds like new worlds seeping out of a digital abyss.

title: Monument
description: On its second album of 2021, the London group fastidiously projects electronic music, pop, and jazz through the twin prisms of post-rock and classical minimalism.

title: Madison
description: Recording deep underground in a West Virginia cave, Haley Dahl creates vivid, ambitious chamber pop with a flair for the grotesque.

Once again, Adele transforms her heartbreak into a searching, graceful, and incredibly moving album. But the complexity of her emotions and the nuanced production make this her most ambitious work to date.

title: Windswept Adan
description: Released last year, this ambitious album by the Japanese singer-songwriter utilizes lush instrumentation to create a dreamlike soundtrack to an imaginary film.

title: Another Side
description: Recorded in 1971, the lost album by the Meters’ guitarist and co-founder plays like a document of what happened, and also what could have happened—a heart-on-your-sleeve acoustic career from a funk icon whose feelings always seemed to be hidden in his riffs.

title: ... EP
description: Equally indebted to no wave and dance, the Manchester, England-based trio’s debut EP walks a fine line between violent and groovy.

title: MP Da Last Don
description: Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the gem of No Limit Records, one that’s as much a flex of power as it is a musical triumph.

artist: Bruce Springsteen / The E Street Band
title: The Legendary 1979 No Nukes Concerts
description: With a setlist structured like a party, this new concert film and live album from a charity gig at Madison Square Garden showcase Bruce and the band at full roar.

title: Bloodmoon: I
description: After 30 years together, the hardcore dynamos hit a nadir. Their collaborative album with Chelsea Wolfe and Stephen Brodsky is exhausting and predictable, a ceaseless barrage of the banal.

title: Al Mundo Azul
description: The New York City quartet’s fourth album is classic and romantic, capturing the liberated frisson of disco and house in an ultra-saturated palette.

title: Raise the Roof
description: Fourteen years after their first collaboration, the unlikely duo reunites for a well-curated selection of covers that spans generations, while adding their fascinating mystique to every one.

title: DEACON’S Grove EP
description: The experimental R&B artist tempers the ecstatic joy of his latest album with a breezy companion EP, offering subtle updates on its plainspoken songs of love and friendship.

title: TwoPointFive
description: The Portland rapper’s buoyant new project sounds like a controlled sugar rush, folding elements of pop and dance into his bright raps.

title: Open the Gates
description: On their latest album, the free jazz collective expands their palette to great effect, channeling the hopes of the past to demand liberation in the present.

title: Music for Psychedelic Therapy
description: Inspired by an expedition into Ecuador’s ancient caves, the vaunted techno producer presents an immersive ambient album designed to accompany guided trips.

title: Son
description: Collaborating with Rosie Lowe, London-based multidisciplinary artist Duval Timothy translates his chordal sensibility to a short but expansive choral suite where sound means more than words.

title: Crawler
description: Exploring personal subject matter and wider musical terrain, the Bristol band’s fourth album plays like the dark origin story for how Idles became the preeminent life coaches of modern post-punk.

title: För Allting
description: On its adventurous new album, the Gothenburg quintet expands on its pitch-perfect blend of post-punk, jangle pop, and shoegaze.

title: A Way Forward
description: The second album from the Brooklyn synth-pop revivalists explores a broader emotional palette while hitting familiar pleasure points.

title: The Death of Speedy Ortiz & Cop Kicker...Forever
